\begin{abstract}
Per-sample error tables, difficulty analyses, sample-level ablations and
per-instance routing all join two artefacts written by different parts of a
pipeline, and they join them positionally. In a widely used forecasting library one
default---validation shuffles, test does not---turns a per-window artefact taken
from the validation split into a permutation of the intended vector, and the fault
survives the usual guards: aggregate metrics and model selection are exactly
invariant, and the vectors are equally long. Our central result is structural.
Under uniform shuffling the permuted table is \emph{equal in distribution} to the
table produced by the canonical shuffled-feature negative control for every
order-symmetric statistic, so a null validated by that control is as consistent
with a broken join as with a true null; when the label is derived from several
independently written vectors, the control instead preserves the label law and no
longer bounds the damage. Two post-hoc diagnostics recover part of the discarded
order---an autocorrelation order test with exact randomisation moments, and a
cross-arm agreement test---but on \NumRuns{} single-GPU runs we map blind spots
rather than only power: the first flags \NumObsAotFlagPct\% of arms in the real
defect yet at most \NumSensFlagPartialQuarter\% of injected block and partial
permutations short of full randomisation, and the second is defeated when two arms
share a loader order, as
\NumObsPermPartialShared{} of \NumObsPermGroups{} real defective groups do. The
primary defence is therefore write-side: a provenance contract that binds each
array to an ordered sample-identifier digest and fails closed stops
\NumContractDetected{} of \NumContractFaults{} injected identity faults, and we
enumerate the \NumContractUndetected{} it misses. Downstream the fault erases a
real association while the headline metric stays bit-identical, and the one-line
repair moves reported test error by up to \NumTaxMaxAbs\%. Contract, diagnostics
and all artefacts are released.
\end{abstract}

\begin{keywords}
reproducibility \sep evaluation pipelines \sep silent faults \sep data provenance
\sep negative controls \sep time series forecasting
\end{keywords}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Empirical machine learning has moved past the aggregate number. A modern paper
does not only report mean squared error on a test split; it reports which samples
are hard and why \citep{hyndman2006}, fits a model of per-sample difficulty,
routes each sample to one of several arms, correlates per-sample loss with
per-sample covariates, and ablates features against a per-sample outcome. Every
one of those analyses consumes a \emph{per-sample artefact}: a vector with one
entry per evaluation sample, written by the evaluation loop, and later joined
against a second table with one row per evaluation sample, written by a different
piece of code---often a different process, a different day, a different author.

The join is almost always \emph{positional}. Entry $i$ of the error vector is
assumed to describe row $i$ of the feature table. Positional joins are the default
in every array-oriented stack \citep{harris2020numpy,mckinney2010}: a shape check
is one line and a key-based join needs a key that nobody wrote down. This paper is
about what happens when the assumption is wrong---when the two artefacts were
written in different orders---and about why that particular fault is unusually hard
to find.

The carrier we use is concrete and widespread. In the Time-Series-Library
family of long-horizon forecasting codebases \citep{tslib,wu2023timesnet}, which
is the de facto reference implementation for a large fraction of the recent
literature \citep{zhou2021informer,wu2021autoformer,zeng2023dlinear,nie2023patchtst,liu2024itransformer},
the data provider constructs the validation loader with shuffling enabled and the
test loader with shuffling disabled. That asymmetry is harmless for its intended
purpose: the validation split is consumed only through a mean. It stops being
harmless the moment anyone stores a \emph{per-window} quantity from the validation
split---which is exactly what per-window difficulty analysis, window-level gating
and per-sample ablation require. The stored vector is then in loader order, the
feature table is in window order, and the positional join silently pairs window
$i$'s features with a uniformly random other window's error.

What makes this fault worth a paper is not that a permutation destroys
information---that is obvious---but the structure of its invisibility. We prove
three things about it. First, the fault is invariant to every aggregate the
pipeline actually checks: the validation mean, the early-stopping trajectory, the
model-selection decision and the headline table are bit-identical, because a mean
is a function of a multiset (Proposition~\ref{prop:invariance}). Second, the
length check that array code performs instead of a key check is blind by
construction whenever the last partial batch is kept, which is the standard
setting for evaluation loaders (Proposition~\ref{prop:length}). Third---and this
is our main conceptual contribution---the corrupted joined table is \emph{equal in
distribution} to the table produced by the negative control that the community
uses to validate exactly this kind of analysis, namely shuffling the feature rows
(Proposition~\ref{prop:degeneracy}). A shuffled-feature control is meant to show
that a reported association is not an artefact of the pipeline. Under the defect
it shows nothing at all: the ``real'' arm and the control arm are the same
experiment, so the control cannot fail. Any statistic that reads the joined table
as an exchangeable set of pairs---Spearman or Pearson correlation, decile
contrasts, $R^2$ of a fitted difficulty model, permutation feature importance,
per-sample gating accuracy---inherits the degeneracy.

The consequence is asymmetric and, we argue, under-appreciated. A broken join
cannot manufacture a positive finding: it attenuates every association towards
the null (Proposition~\ref{prop:attenuation}). It can, and in our experiments
does, manufacture a \emph{negative} finding, and negative findings about
per-sample structure are published: ``window difficulty is not predictable'',
``per-sample routing does not help'', ``these features carry no signal''. Such a
claim, accompanied by a shuffled-feature control that behaves ``as expected'', is
indistinguishable from a silent order bug. We wrote this paper because we hit the
fault ourselves while auditing per-window plug-in selection \citep{companion2026},
where the conclusion under study was precisely of that shape.

The situation is not hopeless, but the recoverable margin is narrower than the
fault's simplicity suggests. The aggregate discards the information needed to
detect the fault; the artefact itself retains some of it. Two
structures survive in a per-sample error vector and are weakened by a
permutation. (i) In sliding-window forecasting, consecutive windows overlap in
$L+H-1$ of their $L+H$ time steps, so consecutive per-window errors are strongly
dependent; the intact vector therefore has a serial correlation near one, and a
uniformly permuted vector has none. We turn this into the
\emph{autocorrelation order test}
(AOT), whose randomisation distribution has exact first and second moments
\citep{wald1943}, hence an $O(n)$ $p$-value with no resampling. (ii) When several
arms are evaluated on the same samples, their per-sample errors agree strongly
because sample difficulty dominates arm identity; if a defective pipeline draws an
\emph{independent} permutation per arm, the agreement collapses. That is the
\emph{cross-arm agreement test} (CAT), which needs no serial structure and
therefore applies to independent and identically distributed data, where AOT has
no signal. Neither test needs the model, the data or a rerun---they read the
published vectors, so a third party can audit an artefact they merely downloaded.

Our empirical contribution about these two diagnostics is mostly negative, and we
report it that way because it is what the data support. Both tests have
sharp operating boundaries, and in this study both boundaries turned out to be
inside the space of faults that a real pipeline produces. AOT keys on the loss of
serial dependence, so it flags a near-uniform permutation---%
\NumObsAotFlagPct\% of arms on our real defective artefacts---but it does not
flag a corruption that preserves long contiguous runs: over injected block
permutations at four block lengths its flag rate is
\NumSensFlagBlockMax\%, and for partial permutations of $5\%$ and $10\%$ of
positions it is \NumSensFlagPartialMildMax\%. CAT keys on the collapse of
cross-arm agreement, which presumes that each arm was permuted independently. We
audited that presumption against our own archive instead of assuming it, and it
does not hold: of \NumObsPermGroups{} real defective four-arm groups, only
\NumObsPermAllDistinct{} have pairwise distinct loader orders, while
\NumObsPermPartialShared{} share at least one order between two arms and
\NumObsPermAllIdentical{} share one order across all four. Under exactly that
sharing structure CAT certifies \NumObsCatCertGroups{} of
\NumObsPermGroups{} genuinely corrupted groups as clean. A controlled sweep
confirms the mechanism: with independently drawn permutations CAT flags
\NumCatCondGroups{} of \NumCatCondGroups{} groups, and with even a single shared
pair among four arms it flags none. The honest reading is that AOT is a
targeted diagnostic for near-random order corruption and CAT requires
independently produced orders; neither is a general integrity check.

That is why the primary defence has to be a write-side one, and why we spend more
of this paper on it than the original framing would suggest. A sidecar that
merely names the order an array is in is not enough---an equally long array from a
different sample set, an array rotated by one, or a stale sidecar all survive such
a check. We therefore specify a contract that binds each array to a digest of its
\emph{ordered} sample identifiers, a digest of its own values, and the identity of
the sample set it came from, and that fails closed when any of those disagree. We
implement it, back-fill it over \NumBackfillDirs{} archived cells, and test it
adversarially: it stops \NumContractDetected{} of \NumContractFaults{} injected
faults, including rotation, arbitrary permutation, stale sidecars and equally long
arrays from a different horizon. It does not stop
\NumContractUndetected{}, and we enumerate them, because a contract whose
limits are unstated invites exactly the misplaced confidence this paper is about.

Finally, we quantify a practical trap in the repair. Removing the shuffle from a
validation loader changes how many pseudo-random numbers the run consumes and
therefore the whole subsequent training trajectory. Across
\NumTaxPairs{} matched pairs that differ only in this flag, reported test error
moves by a median of \NumTaxMedianAbs\% and a maximum of \NumTaxMaxAbs\%, and the
selected epoch changes in a substantial fraction of pairs. A maintainer who fixes
the flag and compares against previously published numbers is therefore comparing
two different experiments, and must re-run rather than patch.

\paragraph{Contributions}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{A named fault class with an exact invisibility argument.} We
formalise \emph{silent order corruption}: a positional join between two
per-sample artefacts written in different iteration orders. We prove that it is
invariant to all order-symmetric aggregates (Proposition~\ref{prop:invariance}),
that the standard length check cannot see it (Proposition~\ref{prop:length}), and
that it attenuates associations monotonically towards the null
(Proposition~\ref{prop:attenuation}).
\item \textbf{Control degeneration.} We prove that the corrupted table and the
canonical shuffled-feature negative control are equal in distribution
(Proposition~\ref{prop:degeneracy}), so the control that is supposed to protect a
per-sample claim is, for this fault, uninformative by construction: no statistic of
the joined table can separate the two arms. To our knowledge this failure
mode of negative controls has not been stated. We verify the equality empirically
with equivalence tests rather than with a failure to reject
(Section~\ref{sec:res-downstream}). We also identify the one case where the two
differ---analyses whose label is derived from several independently written
vectors, such as per-sample arm selection---and show that the difference runs the
wrong way: the control preserves the label law and therefore reports a
\emph{milder} failure than the defect causes (Proposition~\ref{prop:derived}).
\item \textbf{Two post-hoc order diagnostics, and a measurement of where they
stop working.} AOT, with exact randomisation moments and a closed-form power
expression, and CAT, for data without serial structure. We calibrate both against
Monte-Carlo nulls, and we then spend most of the evaluation on their boundaries
rather than on their power: the corruption severities AOT does not flag, the
cross-arm order-sharing patterns that defeat CAT, and---using the observed
permutations in our own archive rather than simulated ones---how often those
adverse conditions actually occur (Sections~\ref{sec:tests},
\ref{sec:res-detect}). We also correct the analytic reference distribution for
CAT, whose earlier form omitted the $\binom{K}{2}$ pairs being averaged and was
consequently mis-scaled by $\NumCatSdRatioNaiveMedian{}$
(Section~\ref{sec:cat}).
\item \textbf{A provenance contract that verifies sample identity, not just an
order label,} with a reference implementation, a write-side and read-side API, a
back-fill over the archived artefacts, and an adversarial test suite. We report a
machine-generated coverage table listing both the \NumContractDetected{} faults
the contract stops and the \NumContractUndetected{} it does not
(Section~\ref{sec:contract}).
\item \textbf{An empirical study} of \NumRuns{} single-GPU runs over
\NumDatasets{} datasets, \NumBackbones{} backbones, \NumArms{} arms and four
horizons (\NumGpuHours{} GPU hours), which (a) confirms on real artefacts that the
permutation is exactly a permutation and the aggregate is unchanged to machine
precision, (b) measures detector operating characteristics and blind spots on
\NumSequences{} real sequences covering \NumWindowsAudited{} window-level
evaluations, (c) shows a
real per-window association collapsing from Spearman
\NumTaskOneRhoIndexMedian{} to \NumTaskOneRhoDefectMedian{} under the defect,
using dependence-aware and cluster-aware inference rather than an
independent-pairs approximation, and (d) quantifies the cost of the repair.
\item \textbf{Actionable guidance} for authors, reviewers and artefact
evaluators, in the form of a checklist tied to the contract and, where a
diagnostic is applicable, to the tests
(Section~\ref{sec:guidance}).
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{What we do not claim}
We do not claim that any published result is wrong. We did not audit other
people's artefacts; we characterise a fault we found in our own pipeline, built on
a public library whose defaults make the fault easy to reach, and we quantify what
it does. We do not claim that the two diagnostics detect order corruption in
general. They were not observed to detect block permutations or mild partial
permutations under the protocol we evaluated, and CAT was not observed to detect
any corruption once two arms shared a loader order; what they certify is the
absence of a specific, near-uniform scrambling, on artefacts of the lengths we
studied, and Section~\ref{sec:limits} lists what they cannot see. We do not claim
that the contract certifies correctness: it certifies which sample each number
belongs to, never that the number is the right statistic. We do not claim that the
fault is confined to time series; the
formal statements only require a per-sample artefact and a positional join, and
sliding windows merely make one of the two diagnostics unusually powerful. All
statistical statements below are calibrated at the sample sizes we evaluated;
where a claim rests on the \NumDepDatasets{} datasets in the grid rather than on
the \NumDepCells{} runs, we report it with the datasets as the resampling unit and
accept the resulting wide intervals.

% =====================================================================
\section{The fault}
\label{sec:fault}

\subsection{Setting and notation}

Fix an evaluation split with $n$ samples. In the sliding-window forecasting setting
that we use throughout, sample $j$ is the window that starts at time $j$: it
consists of a look-back of $L$ steps and a target of $H$ steps, and
$j \in \{0,\dots,n-1\}$ enumerates the windows in calendar order. Write
$\ell = (\ell_0,\dots,\ell_{n-1})$ for the per-sample loss, $\ell_j$ being the mean
squared error of the trained model on window $j$, and $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$
for a table of per-sample covariates, row $j$ describing window $j$. In our
experiments $X$ holds $d = 10$ cheap descriptors of the look-back window only
(volatility, range, mean absolute increment, trend slope, lag-1 autocorrelation,
level drift, spectral entropy, cross-channel correlation, deviation of the last
point from the window mean, kurtosis); nothing in the analysis depends on the
particular choice.

\begin{definition}[Index order and loader order]
\label{def:orders}
An array of length $n$ is in \emph{index order} if its $i$-th entry describes
sample $i$. It is in \emph{loader order} if its $i$-th entry describes the sample
visited $i$-th by the data loader that produced it. The two coincide if and only
if the loader is sequential.
\end{definition}

A data loader that shuffles draws a permutation $\sigma \in S_n$ and visits
samples $\sigma(0), \sigma(1), \dots$. An evaluation loop that appends one number
per batch element therefore writes the vector
\begin{equation}
a_i \;=\; \ell_{\sigma(i)}, \qquad i = 0,\dots,n-1 ,
\label{eq:defect}
\end{equation}
which is in loader order. A downstream consumer that joins positionally against
$X$ believes $a_i = \ell_i$. We call the resulting analysis \emph{order
corrupted}, and we call the fault \emph{silent} because, as
Section~\ref{sec:silence} shows, nothing the pipeline checks changes.

\subsection{How the fault is reached in practice}
\label{sec:reached}

The fault needs two ingredients that live far apart in the source: a shuffling
evaluation loader, and a consumer that joins positionally. Listing~\ref{lst:up}
shows the first as it appears in the Time-Series-Library data provider
\citep{tslib}, quoted verbatim from the copy vendored in our replication package
(SHA-256 \texttt{8034b4a9\ldots ad9a}).

\begin{lstlisting}[caption={The provider that makes the fault reachable, quoted
verbatim. Only \texttt{test} is protected, and the last partial batch is kept for
every split. The flag is correct for its intended purpose---the validation split
is consumed through a mean---and becomes a hazard the moment a per-sample artefact
is stored from the validation split.},label={lst:up}]
def data_provider(args, flag):
    ...
    shuffle_flag = False if (flag == 'test' or flag == 'TEST') else True
    drop_last = False        # kept for every split, including 'val'
    ...
    data_loader = DataLoader(data_set, batch_size=batch_size,
                             shuffle=shuffle_flag,   # 'val' -> True
                             num_workers=args.num_workers,
                             drop_last=drop_last)
\end{lstlisting}

Two properties of this snippet matter. First, the asymmetry is invisible at the
call site: the caller asks for \texttt{data\_provider(args, 'val')} and receives a
loader whose order is a global, undocumented policy decision expressed as a
one-line ternary. Second, the last partial batch is kept for every split
(\texttt{drop\_last=False}), so an evaluation loop adapted to save per-sample
quantities writes exactly one entry per validation window, whatever the order.
Nothing has to be modified for the last accidental guard to be absent: the length
of the saved vector already matches the feature table under both orders, as
Proposition~\ref{prop:length} makes precise.

Listing~\ref{lst:down} shows the consumer. It is four lines, it contains a shape
assertion, and it is wrong.

\begin{lstlisting}[caption={The consumer. The assertion passes, the join is
wrong, and no exception is ever raised.},label={lst:down}]
err = np.load(f"{run}/val_window_mse.npy")   # loader order (unknown to the caller)
feat = build_window_features(dataset, split="val")   # index order
assert len(err) == len(feat)                 # passes: both equal n
rho = spearmanr(feat["volatility"], err).statistic   # meaningless
\end{lstlisting}

We stress that neither listing is unusual, and that the fault is not a bug in the
library: the library never promised an order, and never stored a per-sample
artefact from the validation split. The fault is created by the composition, which
is precisely why it survives code review of either half in isolation. This is the
shape of fault that the software-engineering literature calls \emph{silent}: it
produces no crash, no warning and no visibly wrong output
\citep{tambon2024,islam2019,zhang2018tf}.

\subsection{Why the pipeline's own guards cannot see it}
\label{sec:silence}

\begin{proposition}[Aggregate invariance]
\label{prop:invariance}
Let $T$ be any functional of a vector that depends only on its multiset of
entries, and let $a$ be as in \eqref{eq:defect}. Then $T(a) = T(\ell)$ for every
$\sigma \in S_n$. In particular the validation mean, every quantile, the
histogram, and hence the early-stopping trajectory, the selected checkpoint and
every order-symmetric aggregate computed from the validation split are unchanged.
Aggregates that are not order-symmetric---a per-window plot, a rolling statistic,
or any join keyed on position---are of course affected; the point of the
proposition is that these are not the quantities a training pipeline checks.
\end{proposition}

\begin{pf}
$a$ is a rearrangement of $\ell$, so the two share a multiset of entries, and $T$
depends on nothing else. Early stopping compares scalar aggregates across epochs;
if each epoch's aggregate is unchanged, the comparison is unchanged, and so is the
resulting checkpoint. \qed
\end{pf}

Proposition~\ref{prop:invariance} is the reason the fault is not caught by the
experiment itself. Every number that appears in a conventional results table is
computed from a multiset. The fault lives entirely in the \emph{index} of the
artefact, and conventional reporting never reads the index.

\begin{proposition}[Blindness of the length check]
\label{prop:length}
Let the loader use batch size $b$ and let $n = qb + r$ with $0 \le r < b$. If the
loader keeps the last partial batch, the saved vector has length $n$ for every
$\sigma$, so a length or shape assertion against $X$ passes identically under the
defect and under the intended behaviour. If instead the loader drops the last
batch, the saved length is $qb$ under both orders; the assertion then fails---but
it fails for a reason unrelated to order, and the standard repair is to keep the
last batch, which restores blindness.
\end{proposition}

\begin{pf}
Immediate: the number of visited samples does not depend on the visiting order.
\qed
\end{pf}

The practical reading of Proposition~\ref{prop:length} is uncomfortable. The one
guard that array-oriented code reliably writes---a shape assertion---is exactly
the guard that this fault is immune to, and the immunity is strongest in the
configuration that a careful author will choose.

\subsection{What the fault does to inference}

\begin{proposition}[Attenuation to the null]
\label{prop:attenuation}
Let $\sigma$ be drawn uniformly from $S_n$ independently of $(X,\ell)$, and let
$\hat\rho$ be the sample Spearman correlation between a column of $X$ and the
joined vector $a$. Then, conditionally on $(X,\ell)$,
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}[\hat\rho] = 0, \qquad
\operatorname{Var}[\hat\rho] = \frac{1}{n-1},
\label{eq:atten}
\end{equation}
so $\hat\rho = O_P(n^{-1/2})$ regardless of the true association, and any test of
$\hat\rho = 0$ has size equal to its nominal level. The same holds for any
rank-based or moment-based association statistic that is a function of the
joined pairs and has population value zero under independence.
\end{proposition}

\begin{pf}
Under a uniform $\sigma$, the ranks of $a$ form a uniformly random permutation
independent of the ranks of the covariate column; \eqref{eq:atten} is the classical
randomisation mean and variance of Spearman's coefficient under independence. The
statement for other statistics follows because the joined pairs are exchangeable
with independent margins. \qed
\end{pf}

Proposition~\ref{prop:attenuation} says the fault is \emph{conservative for
positive claims}: it cannot fabricate an association, because it destroys the
pairing that any association would have to be carried by. It is exactly the
opposite of a leakage fault, which inflates results \citep{kapoor2023}. That
asymmetry has been read as reassurance in discussions of pipeline hygiene. It is
not reassurance. It means the fault specialises in producing the one kind of
finding that no positive-result check will catch: a null.

% =====================================================================
\section{Control degeneration: why the standard negative control cannot fail}
\label{sec:degeneracy}

When a paper reports a per-sample analysis, the accepted way to show that the
analysis is not an artefact of the pipeline is a negative control
\citep{lipsitch2010}: re-run it with the association deliberately destroyed and
check that the reported effect disappears. In per-sample machine learning the
canonical instance is the \emph{shuffled-feature control}---permute the rows of
$X$, keep $\ell$, refit, and verify that the signal vanishes; it is the
sample-level analogue of the random-label control used to probe memorisation. It
is cheap, it is standard, and against this fault it is useless.

\begin{proposition}[Distributional equality of the defect and the control]
\label{prop:degeneracy}
Let $\sigma,\pi$ be independent and uniform on $S_n$ and independent of
$(X,\ell)$. Define the \emph{defect} table
$D = \{(X_i, \ell_{\sigma(i)})\}_{i=0}^{n-1}$ and the \emph{shuffled-feature
control} table $C = \{(X_{\pi(i)}, \ell_i)\}_{i=0}^{n-1}$. Then $D$ and $C$ have
the same distribution as multisets of pairs. Consequently, for every statistic $S$
that is a function of the multiset of joined pairs,
\begin{equation}
S(D) \;\overset{d}{=}\; S(C).
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{pf}
Re-index $C$ by $j = \pi(i)$: as a multiset,
$C = \{(X_{\pi(i)},\ell_i)\}_i = \{(X_j, \ell_{\pi^{-1}(j)})\}_j$. Since $\pi$ is
uniform on $S_n$, so is $\pi^{-1}$, and $\pi^{-1}$ is independent of $(X,\ell)$.
Hence $C$ has the law of $\{(X_j,\ell_{\tau(j)})\}_j$ with $\tau$ uniform, which
is the law of $D$. A statistic that reads only the multiset of pairs is a
measurable function of it, so its law is determined. \qed
\end{pf}

\begin{corollary}[The control cannot discriminate]
\label{cor:cannot}
Let $S$ be a statistic that depends on the joined table only through its multiset
of pairs. Then no test that compares $S$ computed on the joined table against $S$
computed on the shuffled-feature control has power against silent order
corruption; its power equals its size for every $n$ and every $(X,\ell)$.
\end{corollary}

The invariance requirement in Corollary~\ref{cor:cannot} is a real restriction, and
stating it precisely is what makes the result usable. A statistic is covered if
relabelling the rows of the joined table leaves it unchanged. That covers most of
what per-sample sections actually report: Pearson and Spearman correlations,
mutual information estimates, decile or quintile contrasts of the loss across a
covariate, permutation feature importance, per-sample calibration curves,
per-window classification of the best arm, and the test-split performance of a
model fitted on \emph{all} rows of the joined table. Each of these treats the
joined table as an exchangeable collection of pairs---the reason they are
legitimate in the first place---and that is exactly what makes them blind here.

The requirement genuinely excludes one family, and we flag it because it is easy
to assume the result is more general than it is. Any statistic that reads a row's
\emph{position} is not a multiset function, and for such a statistic the defect and
the control need not agree. The practical instance is a split defined by position:
a chronological or purged train/holdout split of the joined table
\citep{bergmeir2012}, blocked cross-validation, or any ``first half versus second
half'' contrast. Under the defect the loss values are permuted globally, so both
halves receive a random sample of losses; under the shuffled-feature control the
losses stay in place, so the second half keeps the losses that genuinely belong to
the later period, and the two arms can differ systematically whenever the loss
level drifts across the split. Section~\ref{sec:results-t1} measures this on our
grid: the purged-holdout statistic is the one statistic in the study where defect
and control separate detectably, in the direction the argument predicts. This is
not a weakness of the theory but a boundary of it---and a narrow one, because an
author who chose a position-based holdout to validate a per-sample claim has an
accidental partial guard, not a designed one: it responds to drift in the loss
level, not to the corruption itself, so it fires on some pipelines and stays silent
on others.

Three points deserve emphasis.

\emph{The degeneracy is not asymptotic.} The two laws are equal for every $n$, so
no amount of data helps, and a larger evaluation split makes the null look
\emph{cleaner}, because both arms converge to the same null value at rate
$n^{-1/2}$.

\emph{It survives multiplicity correction.} Reporting a family of features with a
false-discovery-rate correction \citep{benjamini1995} controls the error rate of
the family under the null, which is precisely the situation the defect creates.
The correction behaves impeccably and confirms the wrong conclusion.

\emph{It survives equivalence testing.} If an author is careful enough to
substantiate a null with a two one-sided test procedure
\citep{schuirmann1987,lakens2017} rather than with a failure to reject, the
conclusion strengthens: they will correctly certify that the observed effect lies
inside their equivalence margin, because it genuinely does---for the corrupted
table. We use this in reverse in Section~\ref{sec:res-downstream}: we certify the
equality predicted by Proposition~\ref{prop:degeneracy} instead of merely failing
to reject it.

\subsection{One exception, and it makes the control worse}
\label{sec:derived}

Proposition~\ref{prop:degeneracy} assumes the analysis consumes a single loss
vector. Some per-sample analyses instead derive their target from several vectors
that are produced by \emph{separate} runs---per-sample arm selection is the common
case, where the label of window $i$ is the index of the arm with the smallest loss
on that window. A defective pipeline permutes each of those vectors independently,
because each arm is a separate process with its own loader, and that is a different
object from a single permutation.

\begin{proposition}[Derived labels: the control keeps the label law, the defect does
not]
\label{prop:derived}
Fix $K$ arms evaluated on the same $n$ windows, let $\ell^{(k)}$ denote the
index-order loss vector of arm $k$, and let $A_i = \arg\min_k \ell^{(k)}_i$ be the
derived label. Let the permutations $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_K$ and $\pi$ be
independent and uniform on $S_n$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Under the shuffled-feature control the label vector is $(A_i)_i$ itself,
      joined to the $\pi$-permuted feature rows; its law, and in particular the
      marginal $\mathbb{P}(A_i = k)$, is unchanged.
\item Under the defect the label is
      $\tilde{A}_i = \arg\min_k \ell^{(k)}_{\sigma_k(i)}$. For each fixed $i$ the
      $K$ entries $\ell^{(k)}_{\sigma_k(i)}$ are independent draws from the $K$
      empirical marginals, so $\tilde{A}_i$ is distributed as the $\arg\min$ under
      the \emph{product} of those marginals, not under their joint law.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently $D$ and $C$ are in general \emph{not} equal in distribution for
derived-label analyses: the control preserves the label law exactly, the defect
replaces it by the $\arg\min$ law of independent coordinates.
\end{proposition}

\begin{pf}
Part 1 is immediate: the control does not touch $\ell$. For part 2, fix $i$; each
$\sigma_k(i)$ is uniform on $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ and the $\sigma_k$ are independent, so
the vector $(\ell^{(k)}_{\sigma_k(i)})_k$ has the product law of the $K$ empirical
distributions, whereas $(\ell^{(k)}_i)_k$ is a draw from their joint law. Window
difficulty is shared across arms, so the joint law is far from the product law, and
the $\arg\min$ functional distinguishes them. \qed
\end{pf}

Two remarks on what Proposition~\ref{prop:derived} does and does not say. It does
not rescue the control: the control still has no power against the defect, because
a null remains a null. What it removes is the consolation that the control is at
least a \emph{conservative} stand-in. Since the control preserves the label
marginal, it also preserves the fallback of predicting the globally best arm,
whereas the defect dilutes that marginal towards the product-law $\arg\min$; an
author reading the control therefore sees a milder failure than the defect
actually causes. Which of the two label laws is flatter is not determined by the
proposition alone---that depends on the joint law of the arms---so we treat the
\emph{direction} as an empirical question and measure it in
Section~\ref{sec:res-downstream}, where the modal-arm mass falls from
$\NumLabelModalIndexPct\%$ under the correct join to $\NumLabelModalDefectPct\%$ under
the defect while the control leaves it untouched by construction.

The escape route is therefore not a better control on the joined table. It is to
test the artefact's \emph{order} directly, before any join, using structure that
the aggregate discards. That is the subject of the next section.

% =====================================================================
\section{Two post-hoc order diagnostics}
\label{sec:tests}

We now build diagnostics that read a stored per-sample vector and ask whether it
retains the structure an index-ordered vector should have. The design constraints
are practical: no access to the model, the
data or a rerun; a cost of at most $O(n)$ or a few seconds of resampling; and
known error rates, because a diagnostic without a calibrated false-positive rate
will be ignored. Because the direction of the test is a recurring source of
confusion---including in an earlier version of this manuscript---we fix
terminology before stating anything else.

\paragraph{Terminology}
Each diagnostic tests a null hypothesis of \emph{complete randomisation}. We use
three terms and never interchange them.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Certified structured order}: the null of complete randomisation was
rejected ($p < \alpha$). The vector retains the dependence structure that an
intact vector has. This is evidence \emph{against} uniform scrambling; it is not
proof of alignment, because many misalignments preserve structure.
\item \emph{Not certified}: the null was not rejected. There is insufficient
evidence of structured order. This is not proof that the vector was scrambled: a
short vector, a weakly dependent loss, or a genuinely aligned but
low-autocorrelation artefact all fail to certify.
\item \emph{Corruption detected}: the diagnostic failed to certify a vector that,
in a controlled experiment, we know to be corrupted. This is an evaluation term.
It is only available when the fault label is known, and it must never be used to
describe a verdict on an artefact of unknown provenance.
\end{itemize}
The practical consequence is asymmetric and worth stating plainly. A certified
vector may still be misaligned. An uncertified vector may still be correct. What
the diagnostics buy is a cheap, high-signal alarm on one specific failure mode,
not an integrity guarantee.

\subsection{AOT: the autocorrelation order test}
\label{sec:aot}

\paragraph{Why there is signal at all}
Consecutive sliding windows share $L + H - 1$ of their $L+H$ time steps. Their
targets therefore overlap almost completely, and so do the local regimes that
determine how hard they are to predict. The per-sample loss of an intact vector is
consequently a strongly, positively dependent sequence---empirically, a lag-1
correlation of at least $\NumRMinClean{}$ in every one of the \NumSequences{}
sequences we measured (Section~\ref{sec:res-detect}). A permutation destroys that dependence
completely. Order is not recoverable from the multiset, but the \emph{presence of
serial dependence} is a one-bit summary of order, and one bit is all we need.

\paragraph{Statistic}
Let $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ be the stored vector, $c = x - \bar{x}$, and let indices
be read modulo $n$. Define the circular serial correlation
\begin{equation}
r(x) \;=\; \frac{\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} c_i\, c_{i+1}}{\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} c_i^2}.
\label{eq:r}
\end{equation}
We use the circular rather than the linear form for one reason: under the
randomisation null the circular statistic has \emph{exact} first and second
moments, which removes the need to resample \citep{wald1943}.

\paragraph{Null and $p$-value}
The null hypothesis is $H_0$: ``the stored vector is a uniformly random
rearrangement of its own values'', which is the law of the artefact under the
defect \eqref{eq:defect}. Note that this null is nonparametric and conditions on
the observed multiset, so it makes no distributional assumption about the loss.
With power sums $S_k = \sum_i c_i^k$ (so $S_1 = 0$),
\begin{align}
\mathbb{E}_{H_0}[r] &= -\frac{1}{n-1}, \label{eq:wwmean}\\
\operatorname{Var}_{H_0}[r] &= \frac{1}{S_2^{2}}
\left[\frac{S_2^{2}-S_4}{n-1}
 + \frac{S_2^{2}-2S_4}{(n-1)(n-2)}
 - \frac{S_2^{2}}{(n-1)^{2}}\right],
\label{eq:wwvar}
\end{align}
and $r$ is asymptotically normal under $H_0$ \citep{wald1943}. Writing
$z = (r - \mathbb{E}_{H_0}[r])/\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_{H_0}[r]}$, we report the
one-sided $p$-value $p = 1 - \Phi(z)$,
one-sided because the alternative created by intact overlapping windows is
positive dependence. Evaluating \eqref{eq:r}--\eqref{eq:wwvar} costs one pass over
the vector; on the longest sequences in our study
($n = \NumWindowsMax{}$) the test runs in microseconds. For calibration we also
compute a Monte-Carlo $p$-value by resampling permutations, and
Section~\ref{sec:res-detect} shows the two agree to
$\NumCalibMaxAbsDiff{}$ in the worst case over \NumCalibSeq{} sequences.

\paragraph{Certification rule and power}
Fix a level $\alpha$. We say a vector is \emph{certified in structured order} at
level $\alpha$ if $p < \alpha$, i.e.\ if the complete-randomisation null is
rejected. On a vector known to be corrupted, $p < \alpha$ therefore means the
diagnostic \emph{failed} to flag the corruption. Because
$\operatorname{Var}_{H_0}[r] \approx n^{-1}$ up
to a kurtosis correction, the serial correlation that the test detects with
probability $1-\beta$ is
\begin{equation}
\rho_{1-\beta}(n,\alpha) \;\approx\; \frac{z_{\alpha}+z_{\beta}}{\sqrt{n}},
\qquad
\text{power}(\rho) \;\approx\; \Phi\!\left(\rho\sqrt{n} - z_{\alpha}\right),
\label{eq:power}
\end{equation}
with $z_\alpha$ the upper-$\alpha$ normal quantile. Two consequences are worth
stating because they bound the applicability of the test. Sequences as short as a
few hundred samples suffice when the dependence is strong: at $\alpha = 0.05$ and
$90\%$ power the detectable $\rho$ is $\NumRhoMinNHundred{}$ at $n = 100$ and
$\NumRhoMinNThousand{}$ at $n = 1000$, both far below what window overlap
produces. And the test degrades gracefully rather than abruptly: as overlap
decreases---longer stride, subsampled windows, independent samples---$\rho$ falls
and the test loses power smoothly, which is why we pair it with a second test that
does not depend on serial structure at all.

Equation~\eqref{eq:power} is a power expression against the alternative
``exchangeable values'', and that is the only alternative it covers. A corruption
that leaves long contiguous runs intact---a block permutation, a partial
permutation of a few per cent of positions, an off-by-one shift---does not move
$\rho$ appreciably, so \eqref{eq:power} says nothing about it and the test has
essentially no power against it. Section~\ref{sec:res-detect} measures this
directly rather than leaving it as a caveat, and the measurement is unfavourable.

\paragraph{How deep the normal tail may be read}
The moments \eqref{eq:wwmean}--\eqref{eq:wwvar} are exact, but the normal
reference is not, so a $p$-value quoted at $10^{-6}$ is an extrapolation of a
two-moment approximation and has to be checked rather than trusted. Per-window
squared errors are heavy tailed---sample kurtosis reaches $\NumTailKurtMax{}$ in
our bank---so the randomisation law of $r$ need not have Gaussian tails. We
measured the discrepancy instead of assuming it away. On \NumTailSeq{} sequences
stratified by length we drew \NumTailPerm{} independent uniform permutations of
each, which is exactly the null of the test and exactly the law of the artefact
under the defect, and counted how often the normal rule rejects
(Table~\ref{tab:tail}, \NumTailNullDraws{} null draws in total). The rule is
close to nominal at $\alpha = 10^{-2}$ (worst ratio
$\NumTailRatioTwo{}\times$) and progressively \emph{anti-conservative} deeper in
the tail: up to $\NumTailRatioThree{}\times$ nominal at $10^{-3}$,
$\NumTailRatioFour{}\times$ at $10^{-4}$ and $\NumTailRatioFive{}\times$ at
$10^{-5}$; at $10^{-6}$ the largest observed ratio is
$\NumTailRatioSix{}\times$ nominal, on exceedance counts small enough that the
ratio itself is poorly resolved at this $B$. Across the
\NumTailRatioAboveOneRows{} sequence-by-level cells we measured,
\NumTailRatioAboveOnePct\% are anti-conservative. Levels below $10^{-3}$ must
therefore be read as thresholds on $z$, not as calibrated error probabilities, and
we do not attach an exact guarantee to any of them: what we report is an empirical
calibration at the sample sizes and permutation budget evaluated here.

Two facts keep this from undermining the certification rule, and both are
measured rather than assumed. First, the approximation errs in the harmless
direction: it is optimistic precisely on the long, heavy-tailed vectors, and those
are the vectors whose intact statistic is enormous---no intact sequence with
$n \ge 500$ in the whole study has $z$ below $\NumZMinCleanLong{}$, against a
largest null draw of $\NumTailMaxZ{}$ over all \NumTailNullDraws{} draws. Where
the margin is thin the approximation is conservative: the weakest intact sequence
in the study has $z = \NumZMinClean{}$ at $n = \NumZMinCleanN{}$, and in the
shortest stratum ($n = \NumTailShortN{}$) the realised false-alarm rate is
\emph{below} nominal at every level we can resolve, with a largest null draw of
$z = \NumTailShortMaxZ{}$. Second, when a calibrated deep threshold is genuinely
required, the Monte-Carlo $p$-value used for CAT in Section~\ref{sec:cat} applies
to AOT unchanged, at the cost of $B$ passes over the vector. Our recommended
operating point is justified by this measured separation rather than by a nominal
tail probability, and Section~\ref{sec:res-detect} reports it that way.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Measured tail behaviour of the normal reference. Each row is one
sequence; \NumTailPerm{} uniform permutations were drawn per sequence and scored
with the normal rule. \emph{Ratio} is the realised false-alarm rate divided by the

\paragraph{What AOT is blind to}
$r$ is invariant to circular rotation and, up to $O(n^{-1})$ terms, to reversal;
it is also insensitive to a permutation that keeps long contiguous runs intact, in
the sense that power depends on how much dependence survives. Rotation and
reversal are not idle worries---they are what an off-by-one write or a reversed
sort produces---so AOT must be read as a diagnostic against near-uniform
\emph{scrambling}, not as a
proof of alignment. Section~\ref{sec:res-detect} measures the boundary
empirically with block and partial corruptions, and finds it to be tight: the
diagnostic covers essentially only the uniform case.

\subsection{CAT: the cross-arm agreement test}
\label{sec:cat}

AOT needs serial dependence. Many settings have none: independent samples,
classification, tabular data, or forecasting evaluated on a strided,
non-overlapping window grid. In those settings a second structure is
sometimes available, because empirical papers rarely evaluate one arm. When $K$ arms
(plug-ins, hyper-parameter settings, seeds, competing models) are evaluated on the
same $n$ samples, their per-sample losses are strongly rank-correlated, because
sample difficulty dominates arm identity. If a defective pipeline draws an
\emph{independent} permutation for each arm, the agreement collapses. Whether it
does draw independent permutations is an empirical question about the pipeline,
not a property of the fault, and Section~\ref{sec:res-detect} shows that in our
own archive it usually does not.

\paragraph{Statistic and null}
Let $E \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times n}$ hold the stored per-sample losses, one row per
arm. Define
\begin{equation}
\bar{\rho}(E) \;=\; \binom{K}{2}^{-1} \sum_{1 \le u < v \le K}
\rho_S\!\left(E_u, E_v\right),
\label{eq:cat}
\end{equation}
with $\rho_S$ the Spearman correlation. The null is ``each row was independently
and uniformly permuted''; we draw $B$ independent row-wise permutations of the
observed ranks and report
$p = (1 + \#\{b : \bar{\rho}_b \ge \bar{\rho}\})/(B+1)$, which is exact for finite
$B$. This Monte-Carlo $p$-value is the one we use.

\paragraph{The analytic reference, corrected}
An earlier version of this work also reported a normal reference
$z = \bar{\rho}\sqrt{n-1}$. That expression is wrong: it is the scale appropriate
to a \emph{single} Spearman correlation, whereas \eqref{eq:cat} averages
$M = \binom{K}{2}$ of them. Under the null the $M$ pairwise correlations are
uncorrelated to leading order, so
$\operatorname{Var}_{H_0}[\bar{\rho}] \approx 1/[M(n-1)]$ and the correct
reference is
\begin{equation}
z \;=\; \bar{\rho}\,\sqrt{M\,(n-1)}, \qquad M = \binom{K}{2}.
\label{eq:catz}
\end{equation}
For the $K = 4$ arms used throughout this study the omitted factor is
$\sqrt{6}$, so the earlier statistic understated $z$ by a factor of about
$\NumCatSdRatioNaiveTheory{}$. We verified \eqref{eq:catz} against the
Monte-Carlo null on the \NumCatAnalyticRows{} independent-permutation groups: the
corrected analytic $p$-value agrees with the Monte-Carlo $p$-value to
$\NumCatAnalyticErrMax{}$ in the worst case and $\NumCatAnalyticErrMedian{}$ at
the median, against $\NumCatAnalyticNaiveErrMax{}$ and
$\NumCatAnalyticNaiveErrMedian{}$ for the earlier form, and the ratio of the
corrected theoretical standard deviation to the Monte-Carlo one is
$\NumCatSdRatioCorrectedMedian{}$ at the median. We report
\eqref{eq:catz} for completeness and use the Monte-Carlo $p$-value in all
verdicts, because \eqref{eq:catz} inherits the independence assumption that
Section~\ref{sec:res-detect} shows to be the binding constraint.

\paragraph{Properties and the assumption that matters}
CAT requires no serial structure, so it works exactly where AOT does not. It does
require $K \ge 2$ arms stored against the same sample set, and it requires those
arms to have been permuted \emph{differently}. It is invariant to a permutation
applied identically to every arm, and---this is the part that matters in practice
and that we underestimated---the invariance degrades gracefully rather than
abruptly, so \emph{partial} sharing is nearly as damaging as full sharing. A
pipeline that shuffles all arms with one shared
seed, or that sorts all arms' outputs by some common key, or that merely reuses a
loader seed across two of four arms, retains enough cross-arm rank structure to
pass CAT while being thoroughly misaligned. Conversely a pipeline that scrambles
arms independently on
non-overlapping windows fails CAT and cannot be judged by AOT. The two
diagnostics are complementary in the transformations they cover, which is why we
run them as a battery; they are not jointly complete, and
Section~\ref{sec:res-detect} quantifies the gap.

\subsection{The battery, and its honest reading}
\label{sec:battery}

Given a set of stored per-sample vectors we run AOT on each vector and CAT on each
group of arms that share a sample set, and we report a per-artefact verdict at a
stated $\alpha$. We recommend $\alpha = 0.05$ for a warning and a far smaller
level for a hard build failure: because the intact signal is enormous
(Section~\ref{sec:res-detect} reports a median $z$ of $\NumZMedianClean{}$), a very
conservative threshold costs almost nothing in missed certifications---at
$\alpha = 10^{-12}$ we still certify $\NumCleanCertAlphaTwelve\%$ of intact
sequences, and $\NumCorruptCertAlphaTwelve\%$ of permuted ones---while the sequences
it does fail to certify are the short ones, where the evidence genuinely is thin.
The strict threshold must be read as a $z$ margin, not as a nominal error
probability: our tail calibration (Table~\ref{tab:tail}) shows the normal rule is
anti-conservative in the deep tail on long, heavy-tailed sequences, by a factor of
up to $\NumTailRatioFive{}$ at $10^{-5}$. What justifies a build-breaking threshold
here is the measured gap between the two populations---the smallest intact $z$ we
observed is $\NumZMinClean{}$ (and $\NumZMinCleanLong{}$ once $n \ge 500$) against a
largest permuted $z$ of $\NumZMaxCorrupt{}$---not the nominal level attached to it.

Three things the battery is \emph{not}. It is not a proof of alignment: it
rejects near-uniform scrambling, not rotation, reversal, block permutation, mild
partial permutation, or an order shared between arms
(Section~\ref{sec:limits}). It is not a general integrity test: on the injected
corruptions of Section~\ref{sec:res-detect} the covered region of fault space is
narrow, and on the real defective groups in our archive CAT is inside its blind
spot far more often than outside it. And it is not a substitute for write-side
provenance: a test can only be run by someone who thinks to run it, whereas a
contract fails
closed. We therefore present the battery as a targeted audit tool for artefacts
that
already exist---including artefacts one has downloaded rather than produced---and
the contract of the next section as the primary defence.

% =====================================================================
\section{A provenance contract for per-sample artefacts}
\label{sec:contract}

The fault is a broken assumption about an array's index. The fix is to stop
leaving that assumption implicit. The database and workflow communities have long
insisted that a derived artefact carry a record of how it was produced
\citep{cheney2009,herschel2017,ditommaso2017,koster2012}, and the machine-learning
tooling stack tracks hyper-parameters, metrics and code versions
\citep{zaharia2018mlflow}. What none of them tracks is the one property that a
positional join depends on: \emph{which order the rows are in}. We propose to make
that explicit, and we deliberately choose the smallest mechanism that fails
closed.

\paragraph{The contract}
Every per-sample artefact is written together with a sidecar record. An earlier
version of this work recorded only the order the array claimed to be in, drawn
from a closed vocabulary, plus its length. That is not enough, and the gap is
worth stating because it is the gap a reader would assume closed: an
equally long array from a different horizon, an array rotated by one position, an
array permuted arbitrarily, and a sidecar left behind by a previous run all pass a
label-and-length check. The contract we now specify and implement binds each array
to the identity of the samples it describes.

The record carries: (i) a \texttt{schema\_version}, so a reader that does not
recognise the format refuses rather than guesses; (ii) the \texttt{split}; (iii)
\texttt{n\_samples}; (iv) an \texttt{ordered\_sample\_id\_digest}, a hash of the
\emph{ordered} list of canonical sample identifiers, which pins both the sample set
and its order; (v) a \texttt{value\_digest}, a hash of the array's own bytes, which
pins the array to this sidecar and not to a previous one; (vi)
\texttt{order\_semantics} from a closed vocabulary
(\texttt{dataset\_index}, \texttt{loader\_emission}); (vii) the cell identity
(dataset, backbone, plug-in, look-back, horizon, seed); and (viii) the
\texttt{producer\_commit}, recorded explicitly as \texttt{unknown} when it cannot
be determined rather than omitted.

\paragraph{The design principle}
The point that does the work is not the list of fields but the following rule.
Every sample must have a stable identifier, and consumers must join \emph{by that
identifier}, not by position. For sliding-window forecasting the natural canonical
identifier is the window's origin in the underlying series, qualified by the sample
set it belongs to; we use
\texttt{(dataset, split, look-back, horizon, window\_origin)}, which is
deterministically reconstructible and therefore back-fillable over an existing
archive. Where a positional read is required for performance, the reader must
compare ordered sample-identifier digests \emph{before} reading, and raise on
mismatch. Readers do not open
arrays; they call a loader that takes the \emph{required} order as an argument and
validates the whole record, raising a typed exception on a missing field, an
unrecognised schema, a digest mismatch, a split mismatch, a length mismatch or an
out-of-vocabulary order label. Order-symmetric consumers---anything computing a
mean---explicitly pass
\texttt{None} and thereby document that they do not care. Legacy artefacts written
before the contract are accepted only when the caller opts in explicitly, and that
path warns; the default is to fail closed.

\begin{lstlisting}[caption={The read side of the contract. The default is to
require index order and full validation, so a positional join cannot be written by
accident; an order-symmetric consumer must say so explicitly, and a pre-contract
artefact must be opted into explicitly.},label={lst:contract}]
def load_series(run_dir, name, require_order="index",
                expect_n=None, legacy_ok=False):
    """Load a per-sample array under the provenance contract."""
    side = run_dir / f"{name}.provenance.json"
    if not side.exists():
        raise MissingFieldError(f"{name}: no provenance sidecar; refusing to load")
    meta = json.loads(side.read_text())
    values = np.load(run_dir / f"{name}.npy")
    if is_legacy_sidecar(meta):
        if not legacy_ok:
            raise SchemaVersionError(
                f"{name}: sidecar predates {SCHEMA_VERSION}; "
                f"pass legacy_ok=True to accept it unverified")
        warnings.warn(f"{name}: legacy sidecar, identity unverified",
                      ProvenanceWarning)
        return values
    validate_sidecar(meta, values, require_order=require_order, expect_n=expect_n)
    return values
\end{lstlisting}

\paragraph{The write side}
Producing an index-order artefact from a shuffling loader does not require
disabling the shuffle---which, as Section~\ref{sec:res-tax} shows, has a cost. It
requires recording \emph{which} sample each entry belongs to. We wrap the dataset
so that each item carries its own index, accumulate losses into a preallocated
vector at those indices, and write the result as \texttt{dataset\_index} order; the
loader-order vector and the visiting permutation are written alongside, tagged
honestly, so that the defect can be reconstructed for study rather than only
avoided. The recorder is streaming: it stores one scalar per sample, never the
predictions, so the memory cost is $O(n)$ floats and the artefact for our longest
split is under $100$~kB. Because the canonical identifier is reconstructible, we
were able to back-fill the contract over the whole existing archive:
\NumBackfillDirs{} cells and \NumBackfillSidecars{} sidecars, with
\NumBackfillFailures{} failures, after which every array in the archive reads under
the strict path and every analysis in this paper reproduces bit-for-bit.

\paragraph{Cost and coverage}
The sidecar is a few hundred bytes; the reader adds one file read and two hashes.
To characterise what this buys we injected \NumContractFaults{} distinct identity
faults and recorded which clause fires
(Table~\ref{tab:contract}). The contract stops \NumContractDetected{} of them,
including the transformations the diagnostics of Section~\ref{sec:tests} cannot
see: circular rotation, arbitrary permutation, truncation, a stale sidecar, an
equally long array from a different horizon or split, and a loader-order array
mislabelled as index order. An adversarial suite of
\NumContractAdversarialTests{} tests exercises these paths, inside a repository
suite of \NumContractRepoTests{} tests.

It does not stop \NumContractUndetected{}, and we list them rather than leave them
implicit, because the failure mode this paper is about is precisely a safeguard
trusted beyond its scope. The most important is this: if two producers
independently write artefacts using the \emph{same} wrong loader order, each
sidecar is internally consistent and both declare the same ordered identifiers, so
the contract sees a legitimate join. Nothing in the record can reveal that the
shared order is semantically wrong; only a diagnostic such as AOT, or the raw
dataset indices, can. The remaining four are: an explicit opt-out for
order-invariant consumers of pre-contract arrays, which warns but does not raise;
a positional join truncated to the shorter of two lengths, where ordered digests
are not comparable and only cell identity is checked; a change in the upstream data
or preprocessing, since the identifier carries no hash of the raw series; and a
per-sample value that is computed wrongly but recorded consistently, since the
contract certifies which sample a number belongs to and never that the number is
the right statistic. The contract's other structural weakness is the mirror image
of its strength: it
protects only artefacts written by code that adopts it, which is why the
diagnostics of
Section~\ref{sec:tests} remain necessary for everything already published.
Section~\ref{sec:guidance} states how we think the two should be combined.
