% =====================================================================
\section{Study design}
\label{sec:design}

The theory of Sections~\ref{sec:fault}--\ref{sec:degeneracy} is exact and needs no
experiment. What needs an experiment is everything quantitative: how much serial
structure real per-sample error vectors actually have, whether the detectors'
nominal error rates hold on real data rather than on synthetic draws, how severe a
corruption has to be before it is detectable, how much a real downstream
conclusion moves, and what the repair costs. We therefore run a grid whose purpose
is to produce \emph{artefacts}, not a leaderboard.

\subsection{Grid}

We use \NumDatasets{} standard public forecasting benchmarks (ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1,
ETTm2, Weather, Exchange-Rate and ILI), \NumBackbones{} backbones spanning the
three dominant architectural families---a linear model \citep{zeng2023dlinear}, a
patch-based Transformer \citep{nie2023patchtst} and an inverted-attention
Transformer \citep{liu2024itransformer}---and \NumArms{} arms: the plain backbone
and three model-agnostic plug-ins, reversible instance normalisation
\citep{kim2022revin}, a frequency-domain loss \citep{wang2024fredf} and a
statistics-prediction normaliser in the style of \citet{liu2023san}. Horizons are
$\{96,192,336,720\}$ and $\{24,36,48,60\}$ for ILI, with a look-back of $96$ ($36$
for ILI). Training is the standard protocol of the reference library
\citep{tslib}: Adam at $10^{-4}$, mean squared error, at most $10$ epochs, early
stopping with patience $3$, batch size $32$, and the library's own splits.
Multivariate-to-multivariate forecasting throughout. All \NumRuns{} runs
completed on a single NVIDIA V100 (32~GB) in \NumGpuHours{} GPU hours and
\NumTrainedEpochs{} trained epochs; Table~\ref{tab:grid} breaks the budget down.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{The grid. Every cell is one training run; \emph{arms} counts the plain
backbone plus the plug-ins. Generated from \texttt{artifacts/runs.csv}.}
\label{tab:grid}
\fitwidth{\input{tables/grid}}
\end{table}

The grid has two stages with different jobs.

\emph{Stage E1} maximises the diversity of per-sample sequences available for
calibrating the detectors: all datasets, horizons and arms for the linear backbone,
and a reduced factorial for the two Transformers. Every E1 run uses a
deterministic evaluation loader, so its stored vector is a ground-truth
index-order sequence. This is what lets us measure a false-alarm rate on
\emph{real} data: we corrupt a known-good sequence ourselves and ask the detector
what it says, rather than assuming a synthetic AR(1) model of per-sample loss.

\emph{Stage E2} produces matched pairs. For four datasets, two horizons, four arms
and three seeds we run each configuration twice, changing exactly one flag---the
validation loader's shuffle---and nothing else. The shuffled member of each pair
writes both the loader-order vector and, via the recorder, the index-order vector,
which gives us the \emph{observed} defect rather than a simulated one. The pairs
also answer the maintenance question of Section~\ref{sec:res-tax}: what does the
one-line repair do to the reported numbers?

\subsection{What is recorded}

For every run we store: the per-sample loss vector for validation and test in
index order; for shuffled runs, additionally the loader-order vector and the
visiting permutation; the aggregate metrics; the selected epoch; the wall-clock
time; and the resolved configuration. Every array carries the sidecar of
Section~\ref{sec:contract}, and every analysis in this paper loads arrays through
the contract, so a mis-ordered array cannot enter our own results---an instance of
eating one's own cooking that we consider part of the contribution. Per-sample
features are computed from the look-back window only, never from the target, so
they are legitimate covariates for a difficulty analysis.

\subsection{Analyses}

Two downstream analyses stand in for the class of per-sample claims. \textbf{T1
(difficulty association)} asks the descriptive question a paper prints in a table:
does per-sample loss correlate with cheap per-sample covariates, and how much
harder is the top covariate decile than the bottom? It also asks the predictive
version---fit a gradient-boosted model on the joined validation table and measure
rank agreement on the untouched test split---because that is what a paper claims
when it says difficulty is predictable. We report rank agreement rather than $R^2$
because validation and test cover different calendar periods, so their error levels
differ by construction; and we use a purged holdout \citep{bergmeir2012} inside the
validation split to avoid crediting a model for window overlap.
\textbf{T2 (per-sample arm selection)} asks the decision question: train a gate on
the joined validation table to pick one of the \NumArms{} arms per sample, and
measure the realised test error against the best fixed arm and against the
per-sample oracle. Each analysis is run under three conditions---\emph{index}
(correct join), \emph{defect} (join against the loader-order vector), and
\emph{control} (correct vector, permuted feature rows)---which is exactly the
triple that Proposition~\ref{prop:degeneracy} says must collapse to two.

\subsection{Reproducibility}

The manuscript contains no typed number. Each quantitative claim expands a LaTeX
macro generated from the artefacts, and a verifier recomputes every macro from the
artefacts and fails on any mismatch, reporting the macro name, the printed value
and the recomputed value. Tables and figures are generated by the same script.
The test suite that accompanies the release covers the propositions as executable
statements---aggregate invariance, length blindness, distributional equality of
defect and control, the randomisation moments against brute-force enumeration of
all $n!$ permutations for $n \le 8$, the false certification rate at a nominal
level---so a reader can check the claims of
Sections~\ref{sec:fault}--\ref{sec:tests} without a GPU.

One detail of the analysis layer is worth reporting, because it is an instance of
the class of fault this paper is about and we did not get it right the first time.
Every simulated permutation in the study---the corrupted arm of each detector
comparison, the feature shuffle of each control, the sub-sampling of the
battery---is drawn from a generator seeded by a content-derived key. An earlier
version of our own analysis code seeded those generators with Python's builtin
\texttt{hash()} of the cell identifier. That function is salted per interpreter
for strings, so the artefacts were not reproducible across processes: re-running
the analysis produced different permutations and therefore different numbers,
while every internal consistency check still passed, because the verifier and the
artefacts moved together. The fault was silent in exactly the sense of
Section~\ref{sec:silence}. Seeds are now derived with a fixed cryptographic hash
(\texttt{src/seeds.py}), a regression test asserts that seeding agrees across
interpreters started with different hash salts, and a second test greps the
analysis layer for a relapse. Re-running \texttt{tools/make\_artifacts.py all}
now reproduces the shipped artefacts, and hence every number in this paper,
bit for bit.

% =====================================================================
\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{The permutation is real, and the aggregate does not move}
\label{sec:res-mask}

We first confirm on real artefacts what Section~\ref{sec:silence} proves. In the
\NumMaskChecked{} runs whose validation loader shuffles, we hold both the
loader-order vector the pipeline would have saved and the index-order vector the
recorder reconstructed. In $\NumMaskMultisetPct\%$ of them the two are exact
rearrangements of each other, in $\NumMaskLengthPct\%$ they have identical length,
and the largest relative difference between their means over all
\NumMaskChecked{} runs is $\NumMaskMaxRelMeanDiff{}$, i.e.\ at most the last bit
of a double-precision sum. Every order-symmetric aggregate a reader would see is
therefore identical,
while the vector a per-sample analysis consumes is a uniformly random
rearrangement. Running AOT on those \NumObservedSeq{} \emph{observed}
loader-order vectors---the real defect, not a simulation of it---gives a median
serial correlation of $\NumObservedRMedian{}$ and certifies
$\NumObservedCertPct\%$ of them, matching the behaviour of the simulated
permutations we use for the calibration below.

Figure~\ref{fig:sequence} shows what the two vectors look like. The intact
sequence is visibly a time series with long excursions; the same values in loader
order are indistinguishable from noise; the lag-1 scatter separates the two
completely. This is the entire basis of the detector, and it is worth noting how
much information the aggregate throws away: the two panels have the same mean, the
same variance, the same histogram, and nothing else in common.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figs/sequence}
\caption{One real validation error vector in index order (left) and the same
values in loader order (middle), with the lag-1 scatter of both (right). The two
vectors have identical means, quantiles and histograms.}
\label{fig:sequence}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Detector operating characteristics}
\label{sec:res-detect}

Across \NumSequences{} real index-order sequences (lengths from \NumWindowsMin{}
to \NumWindowsMax{}), together \NumWindowsAudited{} window-level evaluations, the
circular serial correlation has median $\NumRMedianClean{}$ and minimum
$\NumRMinClean{}$: window overlap produces dependence close to the maximum
possible, uniformly over datasets, horizons, backbones and arms. That count is a
sum over sequences, not a count of distinct windows: the sequences are drawn from
\NumSampleSets{} distinct evaluation sample sets holding \NumDistinctWindows{}
windows in total, and each is audited once per run and arm, so sequences that share
a dataset, horizon and split are not independent replicates. Section~\ref{sec:threats}
returns to what that does and does not license. After a uniform permutation of the
same sequences the median falls to $\NumRMedianCorrupt{}$ with maximum
$\NumRMaxCorrupt{}$. The standardised statistic separates the two populations by
orders of magnitude (Figure~\ref{fig:separation}): median $z = \NumZMedianClean{}$
for intact sequences with a minimum of $\NumZMinClean{}$, against a maximum of
$\NumZMaxCorrupt{}$ over all permuted sequences.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figs/separation}
\caption{Separation of the AOT statistic on \NumSequences{} real sequences and
their permutations. Left: the raw statistic. Right: the standardised statistic on
a log scale, with the $\alpha = 0.05$ and $\alpha = 10^{-12}$ thresholds.}
\label{fig:separation}
\end{figure}

At $\alpha = 0.05$ the test certifies $\NumCleanCertPct\%$ of intact sequences and
$\NumCorruptCertPct\%$ of permuted ones. The latter is the realised false
certification rate on vectors drawn exactly from the null; it sits slightly above
the nominal $5\%$, consistent with the mild anti-conservatism of the normal
reference measured in Table~\ref{tab:tail}. Table~\ref{tab:cert} sweeps the level,
and its deep rows should be read as thresholds on $z$ rather than as calibrated
error probabilities. The row we recommend in practice is $\alpha = 10^{-6}$,
i.e.\ $z > 4.75$: it separates the two populations \emph{perfectly} on our data,
certifying $\NumCleanCertAlphaSix\%$ of intact sequences and
$\NumCorruptCertAlphaSix\%$ of permuted ones, and the separation---not the nominal
level---is what supports it. The margin is large: $z_{\min} = \NumZMinClean{}$ on
intact sequences against $z_{\max} = \NumZMaxCorrupt{}$ on
\NumSequences{} permuted ones, and $\NumTailMaxZ{}$ over the further
\NumTailNullDraws{} null draws of Table~\ref{tab:tail}. Pushing to $10^{-12}$
costs sensitivity only on the shortest artefacts:
$\NumCleanCertAlphaTwelve\%$ of intact sequences are still certified, and every one
of the \NumCertTwelveMissSeq{} that are not has at most $\NumCertTwelveMissMaxN{}$
windows---AOT's evidence grows with $n$, and an evaluation split of a few dozen
windows simply does not contain that much of it. A continuous-integration job can
therefore fail the build on order corruption at a false-alarm rate that we can
bound empirically rather than nominally, provided the artefact is not shorter than
a few hundred windows; for shorter artefacts we recommend the Monte-Carlo
$p$-value, whose level is exact by construction.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{AOT certification rates as a function of the level, over
\NumSequences{} real sequences and their uniform permutations. Generated from
\texttt{artifacts/certification.csv}.}
\label{tab:cert}
\fitwidth{\input{tables/certification}}
\end{table}

At the level a practitioner actually uses, the normal approximation is not doing
hidden work. On \NumCalibSeq{} permuted sequences, where the null is true by
construction, the analytic and Monte-Carlo $p$-values differ by at most
$\NumCalibMaxAbsDiff{}$, and the empirical rejection rates at $\alpha = 0.05$ are
$\NumCalibFprNormal\%$ (analytic) and $\NumCalibFprPerm\%$ (Monte-Carlo). Deeper
in the tail it does do work, and Table~\ref{tab:tail} quantifies exactly how much;
the two measurements together are the reason we report a recommended threshold
with a measured margin instead of a nominal guarantee.

\emph{Milder corruptions, and the boundary of the diagnostic.} A uniform
permutation is the worst case; real defects
can be gentler. Shuffling \emph{batch order} while keeping batches internally
sequential---what a batch-level sampler produces---preserves within-block
dependence, and permuting only a fraction of positions preserves most of it. This
is where AOT stops working, and the boundary is sharper than we expected when we
designed the test.

The direction of the statistic has to be kept straight here, because it is easy to
read the table backwards. AOT rejects the hypothesis of complete randomisation. A
block-permuted vector still has almost all of its serial dependence, so AOT
rejects that hypothesis, so the vector is \emph{certified in structured order}---%
which, on a vector we injected a fault into, means the diagnostic did not flag the
fault. Table~\ref{tab:sens} therefore reports the flag rate, i.e.\ the fraction of
corrupted sequences that AOT declines to certify, and the result is
close to zero over most of the fault family. Over the \NumSensNBlockRows{}
sequence-by-block-length cells the flag rate is $\NumSensFlagBlockMax\%$: no block
permutation at any of the four block lengths we injected was flagged, at any
sequence length. Partial permutations of $5\%$ and $10\%$ of positions are likewise
flagged in $\NumSensFlagPartialMildMax\%$ of cases, and moving a quarter or a half
of all positions still only reaches $\NumSensFlagPartialQuarter\%$ and
$\NumSensFlagPartialHalf\%$. Only the fully random permutation is reliably flagged,
at $\NumSensFlagPartialFull\%$.

We draw the conclusion that follows rather than the one we would have preferred.
AOT was effective against complete random permutations in our injected faults, and
it was not observed to flag the block permutations or the mild partial permutations
we evaluated. It should be used as a targeted diagnostic for near-random order
corruption---which is exactly the fault the library default of
Section~\ref{sec:fault} produces, and which is why it works on our real
artefacts---and not as a general order-integrity test. A local or block-wise
statistic would plausibly cover part of the gap; we have not built one, and we
prefer to state the limitation than to gesture at a fix we did not evaluate.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Where AOT stops working. Each row is one injected corruption family;
\emph{flagged} is the fraction of corrupted sequences that AOT declines to certify,
i.e.\ the detection rate. Block permutations and mild partial permutations retain
enough serial dependence that the complete-randomisation null is still rejected, so
they are certified and the fault is not flagged. Generated from
\texttt{artifacts/aot\_sensitivity.csv}.}
\label{tab:sens}
\fitwidth{\input{tables/sensitivity}}
\end{table}

\emph{Cross-arm agreement.} On the \NumCatBlocks{} groups of arms evaluated against
a common sample set, CAT gives median $\bar{\rho} = \NumCatRhoMedianClean{}$,
certifying $\NumCatCertCleanPct\%$ of groups; after \emph{independent} per-arm
permutation
the median falls to $\NumCatRhoMedianCorrupt{}$ and $\NumCatCertCorruptPct\%$ are
certified. \NumCatMissGroups{} intact group is not certified, and it is one of the
shortest in the study ($n \le \NumCatMissMaxN{}$ windows, against a minimum of
$\NumCatMinN{}$ over all groups), where four arms simply do not supply enough rank
information; its $\bar{\rho}$ of $\NumCatRhoMinClean{}$ is the minimum over intact
groups. The agreement is not driven by one dominant pair: across all \NumCatPairs{}
individual arm pairs the median Spearman correlation is $\NumCatPairRhoMedian{}$.
Sample difficulty dominating arm identity is a robust empirical regularity, and CAT
converts it into a test---under the independence assumption, which the next
subsection examines.

\subsection{Whether CAT's independence assumption holds in a real pipeline}
\label{sec:res-observed}

The CAT result just quoted is conditional on each arm having been permuted
independently. We stated that assumption when we designed the test and justified
it by an argument about process isolation: each arm is a separate process with its
own loader and its own random state. That argument is wrong for our own pipeline,
and we discovered it only by checking. Because Stage~E2 stores the visiting
permutation alongside every defective vector, we can audit the assumption directly
instead of simulating it.

Across the \NumObsPermGroups{} real defective four-arm groups in the archive, every
one of the \NumObsPermArms{} stored permutations is non-identity, and all
\NumObsPermConsistentGroups{} groups satisfy the consistency check that the stored
loader-order vector equals the index-order vector composed with the stored
permutation---so the recorded defect is exactly the defect. The permutations are
not, however, independent across arms. Only \NumObsPermAllDistinct{} groups have
four pairwise distinct orders; \NumObsPermPartialShared{} groups share at least one
order between two arms, and \NumObsPermAllIdentical{} groups use a single order for
all four arms. Of the \NumObsPermPairs{} arm pairs, \NumObsPairsIdenticalThree{}
groups have three identical pairs and \NumObsPairsIdenticalSix{} have all six. The
mean rank correlation between two arms' permutations has median
$\NumObsSpearmanMedian{}$ and ranges from $\NumObsSpearmanMin{}$ to
$\NumObsSpearmanMax{}$. The mechanism is mundane: arms that share a data
configuration draw their loader seed from the same derived key, so the shuffle is
reproduced rather than redrawn.

The consequence for CAT is severe. Run on the real loader-order vectors, CAT
certifies $\NumObsCatCertGroups{}$ of \NumObsPermGroups{} groups
($\NumObsCatCertPct\%$) as retaining cross-arm structure---that is, it declares
clean a set of groups every one of which is corrupted. For reference, on the intact
vectors of the same groups it certifies $\NumObsCatCertIntactGroups{}$ of
\NumObsPermGroups{}, so the diagnostic is not merely noisy: it is answering a
different question from the one a user would think they asked. AOT on the same
vectors behaves much better, flagging $\NumObsAotFlagArms{}$ of
\NumObsPermArms{} arms ($\NumObsAotFlagPct\%$) and missing at least one arm in
\NumObsAotMissGroups{} groups, with a smallest observed $p$-value of
$\NumObsAotPMin{}$; the shared-order structure that defeats CAT is irrelevant to
AOT, which reads each vector on its own.

Table~\ref{tab:observed} reports the audit, and Table~\ref{tab:catcond} isolates
the mechanism under controlled sharing. Taking the same \NumCatCondGroups{} groups
and injecting permutations ourselves, CAT flags every group when the four
permutations are drawn independently ($\NumCatCondIndependentCert{}$ of
\NumCatCondGroups{} certified, median
$\bar{\rho} = \NumCatCondIndependentRho{}$) and flags none of them under any
sharing pattern we tried: all four arms sharing one order
(median $\bar{\rho} = \NumCatCondAllSharedRho{}$), three of four sharing
($\NumCatCondSharedKThreeRho{}$), two of four sharing
($\NumCatCondSharedKTwoRho{}$), or two disjoint pairs
($\NumCatCondTwoPairsRho{}$). A single shared pair among four arms is enough. The
residual agreement it leaves is smaller than the intact value of
$\NumCatCondIntactRho{}$, but the Monte-Carlo null is a null of complete
independence, so any residual agreement rejects it.

We therefore restate CAT's scope. CAT is informative when independently produced
artefacts have sufficiently distinct order perturbations. Shared or correlated
loader orders preserve cross-arm rank structure and constitute a blind spot that,
in the one real pipeline we were able to audit, was the common case rather than the
exception. A user of CAT should first establish that the arms' orders were drawn
independently---which, if the visiting permutations are recorded, is a direct
check, and if they are not, is an assumption that cannot be verified after the
fact. This is a further argument for the write-side contract rather than for the
diagnostic.

\subsection{Where each test stops working}
\label{sec:res-battery}

AOT's power comes from window overlap, so we remove the overlap deliberately.
Sub-sampling every $s$-th window reduces the shared fraction of two consecutive
retained windows from $1 - 1/(L+H)$ to $\max(0, 1 - s/(L+H))$, and at large enough
$s$ the retained windows are disjoint. Table~\ref{tab:battery} and
Figure~\ref{fig:battery} trace both tests along that axis. AOT certifies
$\NumBatAotStrideOne\%$ of intact groups at stride $1$ and degrades as overlap
falls; on the \NumBatDisjointRows{} configurations in which the retained windows
are exactly disjoint ($s = \NumBatStrideDisjoint{}$, mean length
$\NumBatNDisjoint{}$) it certifies $\NumBatAotDisjoint\%$. CAT, which never used
serial structure, certifies $\NumBatCatStrideOne\%$ at stride $1$ and
$\NumBatCatDisjoint\%$ on the disjoint grid. Corrupted inputs, pooled over all
\NumBatRows{} configurations of the sweep, are certified at
$\NumBatCorruptAotPct\%$ by AOT and $\NumBatCorruptCatPct\%$ by CAT---the nominal
level, up to the sampling noise of \NumBatGroups{} groups per stride---so the loss
of power at long strides is a loss of \emph{sensitivity}, not a gain in false
alarms. The practical rule follows directly: use AOT when samples overlap, use CAT
whenever two or more arms share a sample set, and treat an artefact that satisfies
neither precondition---a single arm on independent samples---as unauditable after
the fact, which makes the write-side contract mandatory rather than advisable.

\centering

fraction of consecutive retained windows; \emph{clean} and \emph{perm.} are
certification rates (\%) on intact and permuted vectors; the permuted columns
estimate the nominal $5\%$ level from \NumBatGroups{} groups per stride, so their
per-row noise is large while the pooled rate quoted in the body is not. Generated from
\texttt{artifacts/battery.csv}.}
\label{tab:battery}
\fitwidth{\input{tables/battery}}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering

CAT does not depend on it. Permuted input is certified only at the nominal level,
at every stride and by both tests.}

\subsection{Downstream: a real conclusion changes, and the control does not}
\label{sec:results-t1}
\label{sec:res-downstream}

\emph{T1.} Under the correct join, per-sample loss is genuinely associated with
cheap look-back covariates: across \NumTaskOneCells{} runs the median Spearman
correlation between look-back volatility and loss is
$\NumTaskOneRhoIndexMedian{}$ (mean $\NumTaskOneRhoIndexMean{}$), the best single
covariate reaches $\NumTaskOneRhoBestIndexMedian{}$ in absolute value, and the top
volatility decile is $\NumTaskOneDecileIndexMedian{}\times$ harder than the bottom
decile. Under the defect the same numbers become
$\NumTaskOneRhoDefectMedian{}$, $\NumTaskOneRhoBestDefectMedian{}$ and
$\NumTaskOneDecileDefectMedian{}\times$: the
effect is gone, the decile contrast is exactly the ratio of two samples from the
same distribution, and a reader would conclude that per-sample difficulty is
unrelated to the obvious drivers of per-sample difficulty. The predictive version
tells the same story---median transfer rank agreement on the untouched test split
falls from $\NumTaskOneTransferIndexMedian{}$ to
$\NumTaskOneTransferDefectMedian{}$, and the purged within-split holdout from
$\NumTaskOneHoldoutIndexMedian{}$ to $\NumTaskOneHoldoutDefectMedian{}$.
Table~\ref{tab:t1} and Figure~\ref{fig:downstream} collect the comparison.

\emph{How significant is that association, really?} An earlier version of this
work reported that the intact association is significant at $\alpha = 0.05$ in
$\NumDepIidSigPct\%$ of runs, using the standard independent-pairs approximation
$p = 2\Phi(-|\rho|\sqrt{n-1})$. That figure is not defensible and we withdraw it.
The windows are sliding with stride one, so consecutive per-window errors have the
lag-1 correlation of at least $\NumRMinClean{}$ that this paper's own detector
relies on; treating $n$ overlapping windows as $n$ independent pairs
under-states the standard error by a large factor, and it does so in the
anti-conservative direction. This is the same
category of error as the one the paper is about---a statistic that reads a
structured artefact as an exchangeable collection---so we correct it in kind rather
than caveat it.

We replace the figure with two dependence-aware readings, both on the same
\NumDepCells{} runs (Table~\ref{tab:depaware}). Under a circular block-permutation
null with block length $\max(L+H, \lceil n^{1/3}\rceil)$, chosen so that a block
spans the entire window-overlap range, the association is significant in
$\NumDepBlockSigPct\%$ of runs. Under a moving-block bootstrap with the same block
length, the $95\%$ interval for $\rho$ excludes zero in
$\NumDepBootCiExclPct\%$ of runs. The two agree closely, and both are roughly a
third of the naive figure. The block-permutation null is well calibrated where we
can check it: on the defect and control conditions, where the true association is
zero by construction, its rejection rate is close to the nominal $5\%$.

The descriptive effect itself is unchanged and remains the substantive result:
median $\rho = \NumDepRhoMedian{}$ with interquartile range
$[\NumDepRhoQOne{}, \NumDepRhoQThree{}]$ over the \NumDepCells{} runs. What changes
is how much generality that median supports. The \NumDepSequences{} sequences in
the study are not \NumDepSequences{} independent experiments: they come from
\NumDepSampleSets{} distinct evaluation sample sets
(\NumDepSampleSetsVal{} on the validation side) over \NumDepDatasets{} datasets, so
the effective number of independent units is smaller by more than an order of
magnitude. Resampling clusters rather than rows, the median $\rho$ has a $95\%$
interval of $[\NumDepRhoSampleSetCiLow{}, \NumDepRhoSampleSetCiHigh{}]$ with
sample sets as clusters and $[\NumDepRhoDatasetCiLow{},
\NumDepRhoDatasetCiHigh{}]$ with datasets as clusters. The association is
positive under every reading, but its magnitude is not pinned down to better than a
factor of two across datasets, and we make no claim that it would hold at this
strength on data outside this grid.

The one conclusion that does \emph{not} weaken under cluster resampling is the
central one. The paired difference between the defect and the control has median
$\NumDepDefectMinusControlMedian{}$, with a cluster interval of
$[\NumDepDefectMinusControlSampleSetCiLow{},
\NumDepDefectMinusControlSampleSetCiHigh{}]$ over sample sets and
$[\NumDepDefectMinusControlDatasetCiLow{},
\NumDepDefectMinusControlDatasetCiHigh{}]$ over datasets. Both contain zero and
both are two orders of magnitude narrower than the effect they would have to
contain to distinguish the two conditions. Control degeneration survives the
conservative reading, which is what Proposition~\ref{prop:degeneracy} predicts:
it is a distributional identity, not an empirical regularity that could have been
an artefact of the grid.

\emph{The purged holdout was not purged enough.} The predictive arm of T1 fits a
difficulty model inside the validation split and evaluates it on a held-out tail of
the same split, with a purge between the two so that overlapping windows cannot
leak. An earlier version of this work used a fixed purge of
\NumPurgeLegacyOrigins{} window origins for every configuration. That is a constant
where the quantity it has to dominate is not: a single window covers $L+H$ time
steps, and at $L = \NumPurgeBucketSeqLen{}$, $H = \NumPurgeBucketPredLen{}$ that is
$816$. With a purge of \NumPurgeLegacyOrigins{} the origins on either side of the
boundary differ by \NumPurgeLegacyGap{}, so the last training window and the first
evaluation window still share \NumPurgeLegacySharedTime{} time steps, of which
\NumPurgeLegacySharedTarget{} are shared \emph{prediction targets}. The holdout was
therefore partly in-sample at long horizons, and \NumPurgeLegacyLeakCells{} cells
in the grid leak this way.

We replace the constant with two rules derived from the window geometry, and we
report the realised boundary rather than the intended one
(Table~\ref{tab:purge}). Under the \texttt{labels} rule, origins must differ by at
least $H$, so no training label is available later than the first evaluation
decision; at $L = \NumPurgeBucketSeqLen{}$, $H = \NumPurgeBucketPredLen{}$ this
means a purge of \NumPurgeLabelsOrigins{} origins, a realised gap of
\NumPurgeLabelsGap{}, and \NumPurgeLabelsSharedTarget{} shared target points---the
\NumPurgeLabelsSharedTime{} time steps that still overlap lie entirely inside the
evaluation window's look-back, which is a legitimate covariate. Under the stricter
\texttt{disjoint} rule, origins must differ by at least $L+H$, giving a purge of
\NumPurgeDisjointOrigins{} and \NumPurgeDisjointSharedTime{} shared time steps of
any kind. Both rules are verified by interval arithmetic on the actual window
extents rather than by a constant, and the verifier asserts the realised boundary
for every cell.

The cost of doing this correctly is that some configurations no longer support the
analysis at all. Requiring at least \NumDepMinHoldoutWindows{} windows on each side
of the purge, \NumPurgeLabelsEligible{} of \NumPurgeCells{} cells remain eligible
under either rule and \NumPurgeLabelsIneligible{} do not; the excluded cells are the
short-series configurations, all four ILI horizons and the three longest Exchange
horizons, where the validation split holds only a few dozen to a few hundred
windows. We exclude them and say so, rather than shrinking the purge until the
arithmetic fits.

The third column of Table~\ref{tab:t1} is the point of the paper. The
shuffled-feature control---the check an author would run to convince a reviewer
that the null in column two is real---lands on the same values as the defect.
We certify this rather than assert it. A two one-sided test of equivalence
\citep{schuirmann1987,lakens2017} on the paired difference between the defect and
the control, with an equivalence margin of $\NumTaskOneTostMargin{}$ Spearman units
(a fifth of the intact effect), gives a mean difference of
$\NumTaskOneTostMeanDiff{}$ with a $95\%$ confidence interval of
$[\NumTaskOneTostCiLow{}, \NumTaskOneTostCiHigh{}]$ and $p = \NumTaskOneTostP{}$:
on the descriptive statistic the two conditions are statistically equivalent, not
merely indistinguishable. Because cells that share a dataset share a sample set and
are therefore not independent, we repeat the test at the level of the
\NumTaskOneTostClusters{} datasets, averaging the paired differences within a
dataset first; the descriptive verdict survives that conservative reading, with
interval $[\NumTaskOneTostClusterCiLow{}, \NumTaskOneTostClusterCiHigh{}]$ and
$p = \NumTaskOneTostClusterP{}$.

The predictive statistic needs a more careful statement, and we prefer to give it
than to round it away. On the \NumTaskOneTransferTostN{} runs where transfer rank
agreement is defined, the run reported in Table~\ref{tab:t1}---which uses the
loader's own recorded permutation wherever we observed one---gives a paired
difference of $\NumTaskOneTransferTostMeanDiff{}$ with interval
$[\NumTaskOneTransferTostCiLow{}, \NumTaskOneTransferTostCiHigh{}]$ against a margin
of $\NumTaskOneTransferTostMargin{}$ and $p = \NumTaskOneTransferTostP{}$: the
interval brushes the margin and equivalence is \emph{not} certified at the $5\%$
level for this statistic in this draw. The reason is Monte Carlo, not structural.
Both the defect and the control are random draws, so a single-draw equivalence test
is itself a random experiment, and the predictive statistic---which requires
fitting a model per condition---carries far more of that variance than the
model-free descriptive one. Repeating the whole comparison over \NumEqDraws{}
independent draws of both conditions makes this explicit: every draw certifies
equivalence, the largest single-draw $p$ is $\NumEqDrawTransferSinglePMax{}$ and the
median is $\NumEqDrawTransferSinglePMedian{}$, the largest single-draw absolute
difference is $\NumEqDrawTransferAbsDiffMax{}$---inside the margin---and the
draw-averaged difference is $\NumEqDrawTransferMeanDiff{}$ with interval
$[\NumEqDrawTransferCiLow{}, \NumEqDrawTransferCiHigh{}]$ and
$p = \NumEqDrawTransferP{}$. The same replication on the descriptive statistic
gives a draw-averaged difference of $\NumEqDrawRhoMeanDiff{}$ with interval
$[\NumEqDrawRhoCiLow{}, \NumEqDrawRhoCiHigh{}]$. The honest summary is therefore:
the descriptive reading of T1 certifies equivalence under every reading we tried,
including the dataset-clustered one; the predictive reading certifies it in the
replicated experiment and sits on the decision boundary in a single draw, and its
dataset-level test, with only \NumTaskOneTostClusters{} independent datasets,
is too underpowered to certify anything
($[\NumTaskOneTransferTostClusterCiLow{}, \NumTaskOneTransferTostClusterCiHigh{}]$,
$p = \NumTaskOneTransferTostClusterP{}$). None of this is evidence that the defect
and the control differ; Proposition~\ref{prop:degeneracy} says they cannot, for
statistics of this kind, and what these tests add is a measured bound on how far
apart a finite experiment can place them.

\emph{T2.} We stress at the outset what T2 is and is not. It is a probe of how the
fault and its control behave on a derived-label analysis; it is \emph{not} evidence
that per-window gating works. On our grid it does not work even with a correct
join: over \NumTaskTwoBlocks{} groups a gate trained on the correctly joined table
changes test error by a median of $\NumTaskTwoGainIndexMedian\%$ relative to the
best fixed arm---a negative number, i.e.\ the gate is \emph{worse} than simply
keeping the best arm---against a per-window oracle headroom of
$\NumTaskTwoOracleHeadroomMedian\%$. A positive gain occurs in only
$\NumTaskTwoGainIndexPosPct\%$ of groups, and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test
against zero, $p = \NumTaskTwoSignTestP{}$, is significant \emph{in the negative
direction}: the honest summary of the correct join is a reliable small loss, which
is consistent with the prior literature reporting that per-sample routing of this
kind is not learnable. Under the defect the median gain is
$\NumTaskTwoGainDefectMedian\%$ and under the control
$\NumTaskTwoGainControlMedian\%$; all three conditions are non-results in the sense
of Proposition~\ref{prop:attenuation}, which is exactly why the comparison between
them, rather than their absolute level, is what carries information here.

Here, however, the defect and the control are \emph{not} interchangeable, and
Proposition~\ref{prop:derived} says why. The paired defect-minus-control difference
in gain is $\NumTaskTwoTostMeanDiff{}$ percentage points with interval
$[\NumTaskTwoTostCiLow{}, \NumTaskTwoTostCiHigh{}]$, which excludes zero as well as
the equivalence margin of $\NumTaskTwoTostMargin{}$: the defect is measurably
\emph{worse} than the control, so here the equivalence test correctly declines to
certify equivalence (the dataset-clustered interval is
$[\NumTaskTwoTostClusterCiLow{}, \NumTaskTwoTostClusterCiHigh{}]$,
$p = \NumTaskTwoTostClusterP{}$). The label law is where the difference lives. Over the
\NumLabelBlocks{} groups, the per-window best-arm label under the correct join puts
on average $\NumLabelModalIndexPct\%$ of its mass on its modal arm, with mean
entropy $\NumLabelEntropyIndex{}$ bits out of a possible
$\NumLabelEntropyMax{}$; under independent per-arm permutation the modal mass falls
to $\NumLabelModalDefectPct\%$ and the entropy rises to $\NumLabelEntropyDefect{}$
bits, and the share of windows won by the globally best fixed arm falls from
$\NumLabelBestFixedShareIndexPct\%$ to $\NumLabelBestFixedShareDefectPct\%$. The
defect thus flattens the label towards uniform, which is exactly the product-law
statement of Proposition~\ref{prop:derived}. A gate trained on such labels
distributes windows across arms nearly independently of arm quality, and the
realised error drifts towards the uniform-arm baseline, which on this grid costs
$\NumTaskTwoRandomPenaltyMedian\%$ relative to the best fixed arm. The control,
which keeps the label intact and destroys only the features, degenerates to
predicting the modal arm and therefore costs almost nothing. The reading is
uncomfortable and worth stating plainly: for derived-label analyses the standard
negative control is not merely powerless, it understates the damage. We draw a
deliberately limited conclusion from T2---it does \emph{not} establish that
per-sample gating works when the join is correct. Our companion study
\citep{companion2026} examines that question directly and answers it in the negative
for legal feedback delays; the relevant point here is that the two explanations for
a null gate---no learnable signal, or a permuted label column---are not
distinguishable by anything reported in a conventional table, and are
distinguishable in one line by AOT.

\subsection{The repair is not free}
\label{sec:res-tax}

The obvious fix is to set the evaluation loader's shuffle flag to \texttt{False}.
It is the right fix, and it is not a silent one. A shuffling loader draws from the
global pseudo-random stream once per epoch; removing those draws shifts every
subsequent consumer of the stream---parameter initialisation of later components,
dropout masks, and the training loader's own shuffling---so the repaired run
follows a different trajectory. Across \NumTaxPairs{} matched pairs that differ in
exactly this flag, the reported test error changes by a median of
$\NumTaxMedianAbs\%$, a ninetieth percentile of $\NumTaxPNinetyAbs\%$ and a
maximum of $\NumTaxMaxAbs\%$; $\NumTaxOverTenthPct\%$ of pairs move by more than a tenth of a
percent, only $\NumTaxIdenticalPct\%$ are numerically identical, the selected
epoch agrees in $\NumTaxSameEpochPct\%$ of pairs, and a Wilcoxon signed-rank test
finds no systematic direction ($p = \NumTaxWilcoxP{}$). The mechanism is visible in
the split by early stopping: the $\NumTaxDiffEpochPairs{}$ pairs in which the
selected epoch differs move by a median of $\NumTaxDiffEpochMedian\%$, an order of
magnitude more than the $\NumTaxSameEpochMedian\%$ of the pairs that stop at the
same epoch, and the largest movement in the study belongs to the former group. The
repair does not perturb the reported number directly; it perturbs the trajectory,
and early stopping converts that into a visible change. Figure~\ref{fig:rngtax}
and Table~\ref{tab:tax} show the distribution.

validation loader stops shuffling. Generated from

\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figs/rngtax}
\caption{The repair changes the run, not just the artefact. Left: paired test MSE
under the two loader settings. Right: distribution of the relative change. The

\label{fig:rngtax}

The direction of the change is uninteresting and the size is not: it is within
the same order of magnitude as the margins that separate competing methods on
these benchmarks, so it is large enough to move a comparison. The
maintenance consequence is concrete. A team that discovers this fault in a
published pipeline cannot patch the flag and keep the old table---the old table
belongs to a different experiment. They must either re-run everything under the
repaired configuration, or leave the flag alone and adopt the recorder of
Section~\ref{sec:contract}, which fixes the artefact without touching the random
stream. We recommend the second for anything already published, and we note that
this is a good reason for the contract to be a \emph{recording} discipline rather
than a change of loader behaviour.

% =====================================================================
\section{Guidance}
\label{sec:guidance}

The findings compress into a short protocol. We state it as three roles because
the checks that are cheap differ by role.

\paragraph{For authors}
(1) Never write a per-sample artefact without binding it to the identity of the
samples it describes; the sidecar of Section~\ref{sec:contract}---ordered
sample-identifier digest, value digest, sample-set identity---is the minimum, and
an order \emph{label} alone is not sufficient. (2) Load per-sample arrays
through a reader that validates that record and fails closed, so a positional join
cannot be written by
accident; better still, join by sample identifier. (3) If a per-sample artefact
must come from a shuffling loader, record
the sample index alongside the value instead of disabling the shuffle---disabling
it changes the experiment (Section~\ref{sec:res-tax}). (4) Where the preconditions
hold, run AOT on stored per-sample vectors as part of the test suite, at a
conservative level, and read a pass as evidence against near-uniform scrambling
only. Run CAT only if you can establish that the arms' orders were produced
independently; if the visiting permutations are not recorded, that cannot be
established after the fact (Section~\ref{sec:res-observed}). (5) When reporting a
per-sample \emph{null}, state explicitly
which order check was performed; a shuffled-feature control is not one
(Corollary~\ref{cor:cannot}), and if the analysis selects among several arms the
control is optimistic rather than conservative (Proposition~\ref{prop:derived}).
(6) If the per-sample units overlap---sliding windows, nested segments, repeated
measures---do not report significance from an independent-pairs formula; the error
runs in the anti-conservative direction and can be large
(Section~\ref{sec:res-downstream}).

\paragraph{For reviewers}
When a paper reports a per-sample analysis---difficulty prediction, per-instance
routing, sample-level ablation---the question ``how do you know the two tables are
aligned?'' has, at present, no standard answer, and the answers that sound
convincing (a shape check, a shuffled-feature control, a sensible aggregate) are
all provably uninformative here. Asking for the order check is cheap for an honest
author and diagnostic otherwise. A reported null about per-sample structure
deserves this question more than a reported effect does, because the fault only
produces nulls. The useful follow-up is not ``did you run a test'' but ``what does
your artefact record about which sample each number belongs to'', because a passing
diagnostic covers a narrower class of faults than its name suggests.

\paragraph{For artefact evaluators}
Badging schemes check that artefacts run and reproduce the reported numbers
\citep{acmbadging,pineau2021,gundersen2018}. Both checks pass under this fault, by
Proposition~\ref{prop:invariance}. A per-sample artefact can be checked further
without the original authors and without a GPU: AOT reads the published vector,
takes $O(n)$ time, and has an empirically calibrated false-alarm rate at the
lengths we studied. We suggest that
artefacts containing per-sample vectors carry sample-identity metadata as a
condition of the
reusable badge, and note that the check is mechanisable. We suggest metadata rather
than a statistical test as the badge condition deliberately: the metadata check is
complete for the faults it covers, whereas the test is not
(Table~\ref{tab:sens}).

% =====================================================================
\section{Threats to validity and limitations}
\label{sec:threats}
\label{sec:limits}

\paragraph{Construct}
Our diagnostics certify the presence of the structure that order induces; they do
not
certify alignment. AOT is invariant to circular rotation and nearly invariant to
reversal, and---as Section~\ref{sec:res-detect} measures rather than
conjectures---it did not flag any of the block permutations or the $5\%$ and $10\%$
partial permutations we injected. CAT is invariant to a permutation shared by all
arms, and is defeated by \emph{partial} sharing as well: a single shared pair among
four arms was sufficient in every group we tested. An off-by-one
write, a reversed sort, a batch-level shuffle or a reused loader seed therefore
pass. We consider
this a limitation of post-hoc auditing in general, not of these statistics in
particular: content-based inference of order can only see structure that the
transformation destroys. But we no longer describe the pair as covering the fault
class, and the honest summary of our detector evaluation is that the covered region
is narrow and that the real pipeline we audited sat mostly outside CAT's part of it.
The write-side contract is not subject to this limit,
which is why we present it as primary---subject in turn to the
\NumContractUndetected{} faults of Table~\ref{tab:contract} that it does not cover,
of which the important one is two producers sharing a single wrong order.

\paragraph{Internal}
The observed defect is measured on our own pipeline, in which we deliberately
reproduced the upstream loader policy. The corrupted conditions in T1 and T2 use
permutations drawn the way a defective pipeline draws them---uniformly, and
independently per arm---which matches the observed permutations of our shuffled
runs but is an idealisation of any specific real defect. Our T2 gate is one
reasonable design; a different gate would give different gains under the correct
join. That does not affect the comparison of interest, which is between conditions
holding the gate fixed.

\paragraph{External}
The empirical study is entirely within sliding-window multivariate forecasting on
seven public benchmarks, three backbones and four arms. The formal results
(Propositions~\ref{prop:invariance}--\ref{prop:derived}) require only a
per-sample artefact and a positional join, so they transfer verbatim to
classification, ranking, retrieval or any other per-sample analysis; the
\emph{power} of AOT does not, since it is a function of the serial dependence that
overlapping windows create. Section~\ref{sec:res-battery} quantifies exactly how
that power decays, and CAT is the recommended instrument outside the
sliding-window setting. We have not audited third-party artefacts, and we make no
claim about the prevalence of the fault in the literature; establishing prevalence
would require running the battery over public per-sample artefacts, which is
mechanical, and which we regard as the natural next step rather than as part of
this contribution.

\paragraph{Statistical}
The equivalence tests are paired over runs, and runs within a dataset are not
independent; we therefore report intervals alongside verdicts, and where our
sample cannot certify equivalence at the stated margin we say so rather than
reporting a non-significant difference as an equality. AOT's $p$-values are exact
in the first two moments and asymptotic in the tail; the calibration in
Section~\ref{sec:res-detect} bounds the discrepancy against a Monte-Carlo null at
$\NumCalibMaxAbsDiff{}$, and any application that needs exactness can pay for the
resampling.

% =====================================================================
\section{Related work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Silent faults in machine-learning software}
Empirical studies of defects in deep-learning programs and frameworks consistently
find that the most damaging class is the one that produces no crash
\citep{zhang2018tf,islam2019}, and \citet{tambon2024} study exactly this class
under the name \emph{silent bugs}, cataloguing framework-level faults that alter
results without raising an error. Our fault is of that kind but at a different
level: it lives in the composition of two individually correct components, and its
observable effect is confined to an artefact's index. To our knowledge the
per-sample order channel has not been analysed, and the interaction with negative
controls has not been noted.

\paragraph{Nondeterminism and variance in training}
That a training run's outcome moves under changes to random state and tooling is
well documented \citep{pham2020,zhuang2022}, and our
Section~\ref{sec:res-tax} is an instance: the flag that causes the fault also
couples the evaluation loader to the training trajectory. The contribution here is
not the observation of variance but its consequence for repair---removing the
shuffle is not a behaviour-preserving refactoring, so an honest fix is a re-run or
a recording discipline, not a patch.

\paragraph{Leakage, reproducibility and evaluation pitfalls}
\citet{kapoor2023} taxonomise leakage as the dominant reproducibility failure in
machine-learning-based science, and reproducibility programmes and badging schemes
formalise what an artefact must contain \citep{pineau2021,gundersen2018,acmbadging}.
Leakage inflates results and is caught by out-of-sample discipline; the fault we
study deflates them and is caught by none of the standard checks, which is why we
treat it as a distinct failure mode rather than a variant. In time series
specifically, evaluation methodology has been scrutinised for split construction
and dependence between folds \citep{bergmeir2012,hyndman2006,makridakis2020m4};
that literature concerns \emph{which} samples are used, whereas our concern is the
identity of a sample once used.

\paragraph{Provenance and workflow systems}
Recording how a derived artefact came about is the subject of a mature literature
\citep{cheney2009,herschel2017}, is operationalised by workflow engines
\citep{ditommaso2017,koster2012} and experiment trackers
\citep{zaharia2018mlflow}, and is codified for scientific data by the FAIR
principles \citep{wilkinson2016}. Our contract is a deliberately minimal
specialisation: for the single property that positional joins depend on, a digest
over the ordered sample identifiers, a closed vocabulary of order semantics, and a
reader that fails closed. We see it as an instance of the general prescription that
the ML tooling stack currently omits, not as a substitute for a workflow engine.

\paragraph{Testing without an oracle}
Metamorphic testing \citep{segura2016,chen2018metamorphic} verifies programs by
checking relations between outputs of related inputs when no oracle is available.
AOT and CAT are statistical relatives: neither knows the correct order, and each
checks a property that the correct order implies---serial dependence for AOT,
cross-arm agreement for CAT. The connection is practically useful, since it places
both tests naturally in a test suite rather than in an analysis notebook.

\paragraph{Negative controls}
Negative controls are a standard device for detecting bias in observational studies
\citep{lipsitch2010}, and their machine-learning analogues---shuffled labels,
shuffled features, random baselines---are used to validate per-sample claims.
Proposition~\ref{prop:degeneracy} identifies a case in which a negative control is
provably uninformative, because the fault it is meant to detect and the control
itself induce the same distribution. We are not aware of a prior statement of this
degeneracy, and we suspect it is not unique to order corruption: any fault that
acts by destroying a pairing will collide with the control that destroys the same
pairing. That suggests a general design rule, which we state as a question for
future work: a negative control is only informative about faults that act
differently from the control.

\paragraph{Time series forecasting and plug-ins}
The empirical carrier of this study is the long-horizon forecasting benchmark
suite \citep{zhou2021informer,wu2021autoformer,zeng2023dlinear,nie2023patchtst,liu2024itransformer}
and the model-agnostic modules attached to it
\citep{kim2022revin,liu2023san,wang2024fredf}, implemented in a common reference
library \citep{tslib,wu2023timesnet}. We use them only as a source of realistic
per-sample artefacts, and we take no position here on the arms' relative merits;
the companion study \citep{companion2026} addresses the selection question.

% =====================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

Per-sample analysis rests on an assumption that is almost never written down: that
two artefacts produced by different parts of a pipeline are in the same order. We
have shown that when the assumption fails, the failure survives the guards a
pipeline conventionally applies---the sample-weighted aggregate metric is invariant,
the length check is blind
by construction, and, most importantly, the negative control that is supposed to
protect the analysis is \emph{equal in distribution} to the fault it is meant to
detect. A null result about per-sample structure, presented with a well-behaved
shuffled-feature control, is therefore exactly as consistent with a broken join as
with a true null, and nothing in a conventional table can separate the two. The one
class of analyses where the control does behave differently---those whose label is
derived from several independently written vectors---is the class where it is most
misleading, because there it reports a milder failure than the fault produces.

The situation is repairable, but not by the route we first proposed. Write-side is
where the leverage is: bind every per-sample artefact to the ordered identity of the
samples it describes---not merely to a label naming its order---and refuse to load
one for a positional join without verifying that binding. On
\NumContractFaults{} injected identity faults the contract we specify stops
\NumContractDetected{}, including the rotations, permutations, stale sidecars and
equal-length substitutions that no content-based test can see, and we enumerate the
\NumContractUndetected{} it does not stop.

Read-side, for artefacts that already exist, the two diagnostics are worth running
but cover less than their names suggest, and reporting that boundary is the more
useful of our two empirical contributions. On \NumRuns{} runs AOT certifies
$\NumCleanCertPct\%$ of intact
sequences and $\NumCorruptCertPct\%$ of uniformly permuted ones at $\alpha = 0.05$
and separates the two populations perfectly at $\alpha = 10^{-6}$; it flags
$\NumObsAotFlagPct\%$ of arms on the real defect. But it flagged
$\NumSensFlagBlockMax\%$ of the injected block permutations and
$\NumSensFlagPartialMildMax\%$ of the mild partial permutations, so it is a
diagnostic for near-random scrambling and not an integrity test. CAT is
sharper still in its dependence on an assumption we had not checked: it requires
each arm's order to have been drawn independently, and in our own archive
\NumObsPermPartialShared{} of \NumObsPermGroups{} defective groups share an order
between arms, whereupon CAT certifies $\NumObsCatCertPct\%$ of genuinely corrupted
groups as clean. A single shared pair among four arms defeats it. We also found
that the obvious one-line repair
silently changes reported numbers by up to $\NumTaxMaxAbs\%$, so a maintainer must
re-run rather than patch---or adopt the recorder, which fixes the artefact and
leaves the run alone.

Three directions follow. The first is mechanical and, we think, worth doing: run
the diagnostics over the per-sample artefacts that accompany published papers and
measure how often the fault is present in the wild, remembering that a
non-certification is evidence of near-random scrambling rather than of order
integrity in general. The second is to close the diagnostic gap we have documented:
AOT's insensitivity to block and mild partial permutations, and CAT's dependence on
independent arm orders, are both invitations to design statistics that target
locality-preserving corruption and correlated loader state. The third is
conceptual. Our degeneracy result is an instance of a pattern---a control that
destroys the same structure as the fault cannot see the fault---and we expect other
instances to exist wherever a validation device and a failure mode act through the
same mechanism. Cataloguing them would tell us which of the checks we currently
trust are load-bearing.

\section*{Relation to other work by the authors}
This study and the companion manuscript \citep{companion2026} share an
experimental infrastructure and a research programme but address disjoint
questions and report disjoint results: the companion asks whether per-window
plug-in selection is learnable under legal feedback delay, and this paper asks
whether a per-sample artefact is in the order its consumer assumes. To let
editors and reviewers assess the overlap directly we state it explicitly.
\emph{Shared:} the forecasting grid and the trained checkpoints that produced the
per-window error vectors, the dataset preparation code, and the two bug fixes
reported in Section~\ref{sec:res-observed} (the loader-order defect and the corrected
cross-arm variance term), which are reported identically in both manuscripts.
\emph{Exclusive to this paper:} the degeneracy proposition and its controls, the
AOT and CAT diagnostics with their calibration, sensitivity and blind-spot
analyses, the observed-permutation audit of the archive, the provenance contract
and its fault-injection coverage, the dependence-aware re-analysis of per-window
difficulty correlations, and the repair-cost measurement.
\emph{Exclusive to the companion:} everything concerning selector training,
feedback delay, oracle headroom and gating policy. No contribution is claimed in
both manuscripts, and neither manuscript's conclusions depend on the other being
accepted. The two releases are versioned and archived independently, and the
numbers quoted across them are produced by the same verification scripts.

\section*{Vitae}
\noindent\textbf{Mianhan Liu} works on empirical evaluation methodology for
machine-learning systems, with an emphasis on reproducibility, silent data-handling
faults and the statistical validity of per-sample analyses. He designed the study,
implemented the audit tools and the experimental grid, and wrote the manuscript.

\noindent\textbf{Chen Chen} works on applied machine learning and experiment
tooling. He independently replicated the released artefacts and the verification
pipeline, reviewed the statistical procedures and contributed to the manuscript.

\section*{Data availability}
All datasets used in this study are public standard benchmarks (ETT, Weather,
Exchange-Rate, ILI) and are not redistributed here; the release includes the
download script and the checksums we verified. Everything required to recompute
every number, table and figure in this manuscript is released at
\url{https://github.com/oscarliu2019/order-provenance-audit}: the experiment
configuration; the per-run table for all \NumRuns{} runs; the per-sample audit
outputs (AOT sequence statistics, calibration, sensitivity, certification sweep,
cross-arm agreement, the battery); the recovered permutations of the
\NumObsPermGroups{} defective groups and the controlled sharing conditions used to
probe CAT's independence assumption; the per-sample feature tables; the T1 and T2
outputs, the dependence-aware and cluster-bootstrap re-analyses and the purge
audit; the equivalence tests; the paired repair-cost table; the reference
implementation of the provenance contract, its \NumContractFaults{} fault-injection
cases and both diagnostics; the test suite covering the
propositions as executable statements; and the generators for
\texttt{paper/numbers.tex}, all tables and all figures. Per-window error vectors
are released as arrays together with their sidecars, so that every derived
per-sample conclusion can be recomputed rather than merely inspected. A
verification script,
\texttt{tools/verify\_paper\_numbers.py}, re-derives every quantitative claim in
this manuscript from those artefacts and fails on any mismatch, printing the claim
identifier, the printed value and the recomputed value.
